entries.body: Made salmon and rice for dinner, the same basic way I did it back in February when I was terrified of cooking salmon. Skin side down in the cast iron, four minutes, flip, two more. Back then I texted Mom a photo, nervous, waiting for her review. Tonight I didn't even think about it. I just made it while listening to music and wiping the counter. I added a quick sauce this time, miso, honey, and a little lime, which I brushed on at the end so it got sticky. The rice was the good jasmine kind from the big store. Turned out better than expected, but at this point I sort of expected it to turn out well. That's a nice feeling, being confident in the kitchen. The apartment does still smell like salmon. That part never changes. Windows open, it's 30 degrees.
entries.highlight: Cooked salmon confidently with a new miso glaze, remembering how nervous they were the first time in February.

entries.title: Hosted my first dinner at the new place
entries.body: Last night I hosted my first real dinner party, at the new apartment, for five people. Sam, Alex, Robin, Priya, and me. I've never hosted anything bigger than takeout for two before. I made a big pot of Mom's red chili with cornbread, a green salad, and the apple pie with the lattice crust, my Thanksgiving recipe. Everyone sat on the couch and the floor, because I only have four chairs, and Priya brought two more from her place across the hall. Alex hung the string lights again, which have stayed up since moving day. The highlight was when Sam stood up and gave a toast to the apartment with good light and the person who finally deserved it, which made me tear up into my chili. Today, I hung Mom's botanical print from the museum. Every wall has something now. This feels like home.
entries.highlight: Hosted a first dinner party for five friends at the new apartment, a sign it truly feels like home.

entries.title: Onboarding redesign is officially a thing
entries.body: Caught the 8:05, which showed up fifteen minutes late because of ice on the tracks. Got in just in time for the end-of-year all-hands. The CEO announced the big initiatives for next year, and number two on the list was the onboarding redesign, the one Dana told me about in September. The slide said owner, TBD, Q2. TBD. I stared at those three letters for the rest of the meeting. Afterward Marcus leaned over and whispered, that's yours, right? I said I don't know. He said, well, do you want it? And I said yes, kind of too fast. He said, then tell someone who isn't me. I keep thinking about that. I've been dropping hints to Dana since September, little ones. Maybe hints aren't enough. Maybe I need to be as direct as I was with empty states. I'll think about it over the holidays.
entries.favorite: Marcus asking do you want it
entries.highlight: Learned at the all-hands that the onboarding redesign is a top initiative with no owner yet, and realized they want to lead it.

entries.title: First swim in two weeks
entries.body: Did a swim before work for the first time in two weeks. Getting out the door in the dark at 6:10 was the hardest part of the whole day, by far. It was 14 degrees and the sidewalk was icy and every single cell in my body wanted to go back to bed. But I made it, and the pool was warm and almost empty, just me and the flowered swim cap woman, who I now know is named Bev, because she said, haven't seen you in a while, and introduced herself. I felt slow but I showed up. Twenty-four laps, fewer than in October. My arms were tired after ten. But the whole morning had a little glow to it, the kind you only get from doing the hard thing first. I'm in a slump, I know that. But I'm still showing up sometimes. Bev noticed.
entries.highlight: Returned to the pool after a two-week gap in the winter slump and met a fellow regular swimmer, Bev.

entries.title: Cookies across the hall and down the stairs
entries.body: Spent the day doing holiday stuff at home. In the morning, I wrapped all the gifts, which are all done and came in at $284, under my $300 budget. That is a first in my entire adult life. Then I baked two batches of Mom's ginger cookies, the ones with the crinkly sugar tops, and made little plates for the neighbors. One for Priya, who's working a night shift, so I left it on her door with a note. One for the trumpet guy on the third floor, whose name turns out to be Gerald, and who said thank you and then played me a short Christmas song on the trumpet right there in the stairwell. I didn't know what to do, so I just stood there and clapped at the end. One for the older couple on the first floor. I've lived here less than four months and already know four neighbors by name.
entries.highlight: Wrapped gifts under budget and delivered homemade cookies to neighbors, including a trumpet-playing neighbor named Gerald.

entries.title: Last shipping day at the post office
entries.body: Ran errands after work. Post office first, because today was the last day to ship for Christmas, and the line was out the door and around the corner, all the way past the dry cleaner. I waited forty minutes behind a woman with nine boxes. The post office cat was not there today, maybe because she has better sense than all of us. I shipped a gift to Alex and Robin, who are going to Robin's family this year. Then the pharmacy, where I refilled my prescription so I'm not without it over the holidays, which is a lesson I learned the hard way two years ago. Then the corner store for a box of clementines for the train. Mailed, refilled, and stocked for the train. Home by 7:15 and made a frozen chili from the freezer stash. The plan works.
entries.highlight: Shipped a holiday gift on the last mailing day and refilled a prescription before the holidays.

entries.title: Couch WFH, onboarding notes
entries.body: Worked from home today, and the office is basically closed in spirit anyway. Did the year-end design review deck from the couch, with my laptop on a pillow, which my back is now very upset about. Did laundry between calls. Folded it while on mute in a meeting, which I'm a little ashamed of. Ate lunch at my desk again, or at my couch, which counts the same way. But the real thing I did today was something I wasn't asked to do: I started a document called onboarding thoughts. It's just a list for now. All the problems I've seen in our onboarding flow over three years, the screens from empty states, the seven steps that should be three, the spec I wrote last January. Eleven pages already. I don't know what it's for yet. But if TBD comes calling, I want to be ready.
entries.highlight: Worked from home and started a personal document collecting ideas for the onboarding redesign.

entries.title: Christmas cards and a knee wrap
entries.body: Christmas at my parents' again. The train up yesterday was packed, and I sat next to a little boy who explained the entire plot of a dinosaur movie to me in detail. Mom made her usual feast: the ham, the scalloped potatoes, the green beans with crispy onions from a can, which I have learned to love ironically and then sincerely. I gave Dad the knee wrap and he put it on right away, over his pajamas. I gave Mom the raised bed book, and she read it all afternoon and started sketching a raised bed on a napkin. She says she wants to build one in the spring and that I'm helping, which wasn't really a question. They gave me a Dutch oven, a big red one, which is another message, but a nicer one this time. Gin rummy until midnight. Dad won five games. Mom won two. I won zero.
entries.favorite: Dad wearing the knee wrap over his pajamas
entries.highlight: Spent Christmas at their parents' with gifts including a knee wrap for Dad and a gardening book for Mom, followed by cards.

entries.title: Same block as last year, longer
entries.body: Ran around my parents' block this morning, the same route I ran last year the day after Thanksgiving, in Dad's old windbreaker, when I could only run six minutes before walking. I wore the same windbreaker today on purpose. It still smells like the garage. It was 26 degrees and there was a little snow on the edges of the sidewalks. I ran twenty minutes without stopping, then walked ten, to make the thirty. That's not my best. I ran two miles straight in June. But I've barely run since the move, and I was frankly afraid I'd be back to six minutes. I wasn't. Some of it stayed. Dad was waiting at the kitchen window when I got back, with coffee for me, in his knee wrap. He said, farther than last year? Yeah, Dad. Farther.
entries.favorite: Dad waiting with coffee in his knee wrap
entries.highlight: Ran twenty minutes nonstop on the same route where they could only run six minutes a year earlier.

entries.title: Returning the duplicate scarf
entries.body: Back home, doing post-Christmas errands. Sam and Robin both gave me the same scarf, in the same color, from the same store, which made all of us laugh over text. So I returned one at the mall, where the returns line snaked past three stores, full of people holding gift bags with a defeated look. Got store credit, which I immediately used on a nice set of wooden spoons, because I now have a Dutch oven and a cast iron pan and I needed better spoons for them, apparently. Then the pharmacy, where they were out of my prescription and told me to come back tomorrow, which is a first. Then the grocery store for the basics. Crossed three things off the list, if you count the pharmacy as a partial. It's quiet in the city this week. I like it.
entries.highlight: Ran post-holiday errands, returning a duplicate scarf gift and buying wooden spoons for new cookware.

entries.title: Client call in an empty office
entries.body: The 8:05 was late again, fifteen minutes, which is now the standard for December. Cleared my inbox on the platform, which didn't take long because nobody is sending emails this week. Got in just in time for a client call with a big customer who wanted to give us feedback on onboarding. Dana's out, so she asked me to take it, which is the first time I've run a client call alone. The customer's main complaint was that their new employees get lost in our product the first week and give up. That's basically what's in my eleven page document. I took a lot of notes. I tried not to look too excited, since they were complaining. After the call, I sent Dana a short summary, and at the bottom I wrote, I have a lot of thoughts on this, when you're back.
entries.highlight: Ran a client feedback call alone for the first time, which reinforced their ideas about the onboarding redesign.

entries.title: Year-end deck and a hint to Dana
entries.body: Spent the morning on the year-end design review deck. Muting Slack was easy, since only four people are online this week, and the draft was done by 11:30. It covers empty states phases one and two, the hiring we did, and Chloe's growth, with her permission. Writing it, I realized how different this year was from last year. Last year's deck had one slide about design impact, slide seven, and I was nervous about it. This year, the whole deck is design impact. Dana replied to my message from yesterday: let's talk in January. That's it. Not a yes. But not nothing. I'm trying not to read too much into it. Left right at 5:30 and walked the lake path in the dark. The lighthouse was blinking green, every four seconds, still.
entries.favorite: The whole deck being design impact
entries.highlight: Finished the year-end design deck and reflected on how much more impact they had this year than last.

entries.title: New year goals, round two
entries.body: New Year's Day. I took last year's index card off the fridge, still under the pizza place magnet, and graded it. Run a 5K: no. I got to two miles, and then the move happened. Cook more: yes, absolutely, I have a Dutch oven and opinions about broth. Save more: yes, I moved, and the emergency fund is at $2,300. Stop eating lunch at my desk: no, to be fair. Better, but no. Two out of four. So I wrote a new card. One: run a real 5K, for real this time, before summer. Two: emergency fund at three months of expenses by the end of the year. Three: lunch away from my desk at least three days a week, which is more realistic than never. Four: lead something big at work. I couldn't write that last year. This year I could, and I didn't even hesitate.
entries.favorite: Writing lead something big without hesitating
entries.highlight: Graded last year's goals as two out of four, then wrote new ones, including running a 5K and leading something big at work.

entries.title: The big January restock
entries.body: Did the weekly grocery run after coffee, and it was a big one, because my fridge was basically empty after the holidays. Frozen berries, two loaves of bread, salmon, chicken thighs, rice, oats, eggs, spinach, onions, garlic, carrots, celery, a big bag of lentils, canned tomatoes, low sodium broth, yogurt, coffee, and a block of parmesan that cost more than I'd like to say. $103. That's high, but it's restocking from zero, and I'm going to make soup in the new Dutch oven tomorrow, so the lentils and carrots are an investment. I almost bought the expensive cookies by the register, and then remembered I still have half a tin of Mom's ginger cookies at home. Saved $6. I'm the kind of person who calculates money saved on cookies now. I'm not sure if that's growth or a problem.
entries.highlight: Restocked an empty fridge after the holidays with a $103 grocery run, planning soup in the new Dutch oven.

entries.title: Metrics morning, two years running
entries.body: First Monday back. Blocked off the morning for the quarterly metrics write-up and kept it. Turned off Slack for two hours. I've done this exact thing every quarter for over a year now, and it's starting to feel like my own small tradition, the quarterly metrics morning. Draft done by noon. The empty states numbers are holding steady, and Ravi helped me add a chart about first week drop-off for new users, which is the onboarding problem, really. I put it in on purpose. If people are going to talk about onboarding this year, I want my name connected to the data. I'm being a little strategic, I guess, which feels new. The train home was packed with everyone back from vacation, coughing and complaining. I stood the whole way. It's okay. I was thinking about the chart.
entries.highlight: Wrote the quarterly metrics report and strategically added data highlighting the onboarding problem.

entries.title: Bug triage deadline, Friday night
entries.body: Stayed late to finish the bug triage before the quarterly cleanup deadline. There were sixty-two open design bugs, which is embarrassing, partly because I'm the one who's supposed to be doing the weekly Tuesday sweeps since that December 1:1 with Dana, and I let them slide in the fall. So this one's on me. I ordered takeout to my desk, pad thai, the classic, and sent the last ticket at 8:30. Then I realized it was Friday and I'd been sitting in the same chair since 9am. My back is complaining. I'm in the winter slump, too. I haven't been to the gym since the swim with Bev, more than three weeks ago, and I can feel it, in my energy and my mood. I'm not going to fix that tonight. Tonight I'm going to take a bath. But I'm noticing it. That's step one.
entries.highlight: Worked late to clear a backlog of design bugs and acknowledged a winter slump with no gym visits in three weeks.

entries.title: Fifty-eight dollars and lentil soup
entries.body: Went to the grocery store at 8:15 before it got busy. Stuck to the list for once. I've stopped saying for once, actually, because it's been every week since about last March. Rice, frozen berries, chicken thighs, coffee, apples, broccoli, yogurt, and a lemon. $58. Then I made lentil soup in the Dutch oven, which is the same soup I tried to meal prep back in November 2024, the watery one, the one Marcus thought I was drinking from a mug. This version had onions, carrots, celery, garlic, cumin, a can of tomatoes, a squeeze of lemon at the end, and the right amount of broth. It was thick and good. Took an hour. I portioned out five lunches and froze two more. I texted Marcus a photo with the caption, not a mug.
entries.highlight: Made a much better version of the lentil soup that came out watery over a year ago and prepped lunches for the week.

entries.title: Nico asks about the winter
entries.body: Haircut on my lunch break with Nico. Went a little shorter than usual, which is a bad choice in January, but I needed the reset. I've been feeling flat. Nico asked how I was doing, and I said fine, and he said, you're talking slow again. Like February. He's the only person who notices that. So I told him the truth. The winter's been heavy. I stopped going to the gym, I'm ordering in more, and work has this big thing I want but I don't know how to ask for it. Nico kept cutting and said, my grandfather used to say winter is for planning, spring is for doing. I think he made that up on the spot. But it helped. $40. Feel like a new person, or at least a person with a plan to make a plan.
entries.favorite: Winter is for planning, spring is for doing
entries.highlight: Got a haircut and opened up to barber Nico about feeling flat this winter, and he offered an encouraging saying.

entries.title: Dad's physical therapist, Deshawn
entries.body: Day off for the holiday. Called Mom in the afternoon and she put Dad on right away, because Dad wanted to tell me about physical therapy himself. He's had three sessions now. His physical therapist is a guy named Deshawn, who used to play college football and, Dad says, is very polite but completely merciless. Dad has a sheet of exercises taped to the fridge, right where my goals card would be. Leg raises, little squats holding the counter, and something with a resistance band that he says makes him look ridiculous. Mom says he does them every single morning, at 7am, while complaining the whole time, and it's the most consistent she's ever seen him. I told Dad I'm in a slump with the gym, and he said, if I can do leg raises in my pajamas, you can go swim. Fair point, Dad.
entries.favorite: Dad saying if I can, you can
entries.highlight: Heard from Dad about starting physical therapy with a demanding therapist, and he encouraged Jordan to get back to the gym.

entries.title: Priya's dal on a snow night
entries.body: Priya had a night off and invited me over for dinner at her place, across the hall, which is the shortest commute to dinner I've ever had. It snowed about six inches today, so it was perfect timing. She made her mom's dal with rice and a cucumber raita, and a spicy pickle from a jar her mom mailed from Toronto. I brought the rest of the ginger cookies. Her apartment is the mirror image of mine, and her herbs are all inside now, lined up on every window. We talked about the winter. She said night shift nurses all have a theory about winter, which is that you can't wait for motivation, you just build a routine and let it carry you. That's the opposite of what I've been doing. We stayed up until midnight talking and laughing about Gerald's trumpet. Walked fifteen steps home.
entries.highlight: Had dinner at neighbor Priya's apartment on a snowy night and got advice about building routines in winter.

entries.title: Bought real snow boots after slipping
entries.body: Slipped on the ice outside the building this morning, a full cartoon slip, feet in the air, landing on my back. I'm okay, just a bruise. The older man from the first floor saw it from his window and gave me a thumbs up, which was kind and also humiliating. So I finally went and bought real snow boots, the kind with deep treads, after wearing running shoes through two winters like a fool. $89 on sale. Then the pharmacy for my prescription, which they had this time, and a bag of ice melt for the front steps, since our landlord is slow with it. Spread it on the steps myself. Gerald came down and helped. Boots bought, steps salted, and nobody else is falling on my watch. I wore the new boots for a walk to the lake in the afternoon and didn't slip once. They're very ugly. I love them.
entries.highlight: Slipped on ice, then bought proper snow boots and helped salt the building's front steps with a neighbor.

entries.title: Onboarding kickoff all-hands
entries.body: All-hands this morning, and it ran long, as always. The onboarding redesign had its own section. They want a lead named by the end of Q2, someone who can run it from discovery to launch by the fall. Back-to-back calls until lunch. Frankly, half the all-hands could have been an email. But not the onboarding part. Afterward, in the hallway, Dana said, did you hear the part about the lead? I said yes. She said, good. And then she walked away. I stood there not knowing what to do with good. I talked to Chloe about it at our mentoring session, which might be weird, since I'm her mentor. But she said something smart: you told me to ask directly for feedback, so maybe you should ask directly for this. I laughed, because she's right. The train home was packed.
entries.favorite: Chloe giving me my own advice
entries.highlight: Heard the onboarding redesign needs a lead by Q2, and mentee Chloe encouraged Jordan to ask for it directly.

entries.title: The tailor saved my winter coat
entries.body: Ran errands after work. The zipper on my good winter coat broke last week, and I was about to buy a new coat, but Priya told me about a tailor on the next block, an older woman named Mrs. Lin who works in a shop the size of a closet. She replaced the zipper in two days for $28. A new coat would have been $200. Picked it up tonight and it's better than new. Then the pharmacy, where I refilled my prescription while I was there, and finally the dry cleaner to pick up my one nice shirt, which I need for something called a leadership offsite next week that Dana invited me to. Three stops, and one coat saved from the landfill. Mrs. Lin told me to come back anytime something breaks. I like that this neighborhood has people who fix things instead of throwing them away.
entries.favorite: Mrs. Lin fixing the zipper for $28
entries.highlight: Had a winter coat zipper repaired by a local tailor for $28 instead of buying a new coat.

entries.title: Sam's second-round interview
entries.body: Dinner with Sam at a ramen place near Sam's apartment. It was snowing again and the restaurant windows were all fogged up. Sam has a second-round interview this week at a climate nonprofit, the kind of place Sam has been talking about since September. It's a communications job, and Sam would be writing about clean energy instead of writing reports nobody reads. We practiced interview questions over the ramen. Sam asked me what my biggest weakness was, as a joke, and I said not asking for what I want, and Sam said, that's not a joke, and I said, I know. We stayed until the staff started mopping. Sam said that if this one doesn't work out, they'll keep going. I believe them. It's been five months and Sam hasn't given up once. That's a lot of patience. Mom would approve. Garlic patience.
entries.highlight: Helped Sam prepare for a second-round interview at a climate nonprofit over a long ramen dinner.

entries.title: Told Alex about the slump, signed up
entries.body: Got coffee with Alex this morning and we did our usual two laps of the block. Alex talked about the new job responsibilities from the promotion, which are mostly more meetings. Then Alex asked how I was, and instead of saying fine, I told Alex the truth. I'm in a winter slump. I haven't been to the gym in a month. I'm ordering in more. I set a goal to run a 5K and I'm further from it than in June. And Alex just said, okay, so what's the smallest step? And right there on the sidewalk, I pulled up the spring 5K by the lake, the one on April 26th, and signed up. $35. Alex signed up too, on the spot, even though Alex hates running. That's friendship. Alex also reminded me the proposal is in March, and I'm still sworn to secrecy. Twelve weeks. I can do twelve weeks.
entries.favorite: Alex signing up on the spot
entries.highlight: Opened up to Alex about a winter slump and signed up for a spring 5K race together, a turning point.

entries.title: My sprint planning format worked
entries.body: The 8:05 was late, as is its winter custom, so I walked in with my coat still on just as sprint planning started. It was the first one using the new format I drafted back in November, the one Dana said I could do as homework. Tickets estimated before the meeting, and the meeting only for the ones we disagree about. It took forty-one minutes. Forty-one. Last time it took almost three hours. Marcus actually applauded at the end, slowly, like in a movie. Elena asked if we could use the format for her other team. It's such a small thing, a meeting format. But it's the first time I've changed how the team works instead of just what it builds. I think that's what Dana means when she talks about ownership. Also, I went to the pool last night. First time in a month. Twenty laps. Bev was there.
entries.highlight: Ran the first sprint planning using a new format they designed, cutting the meeting from nearly three hours to 41 minutes.

entries.title: January: slump spending, frankly
entries.body: Budget check-in for January. Eating out was $268. Too much, and I know why: the slump. But groceries stayed at $231, because of the lentil soup and the freezer meals. The emergency fund is at $2,700. I'm about a quarter of the way to three months of expenses. I did something different this month, though. I looked at the takeout orders, and almost all of them were on Tuesday and Thursday nights, the days I get home latest. So instead of a general rule about takeout, I'm making Tuesdays and Thursdays freezer nights, where dinner is already made. It's more specific. Last year, I would have just said, eat out less, and then felt bad. This year, I'm looking for the pattern. That's more useful than guilt. Also, the race training plan starts tomorrow. Eleven weeks to race day.
entries.favorite: Looking for the pattern instead of guilt
entries.highlight: Reviewed January spending, spotted that takeout clustered on late nights, and made those designated freezer-meal nights.

entries.title: A freezer inventory taped to the door
entries.body: Spent the evening organizing the freezer and the pantry, because Tuesdays and Thursdays are freezer nights now, and that only works if I know what's in there. I took everything out and made a list: four portions of white chicken chili, two lentil soups, six pesto cubes, one container of Mom's tomato sauce, a bag of dumplings, and a mystery container that turned out to be the turkey congee from December, still good. I wrote the list on a sheet of paper and taped it to the freezer door, with little boxes to cross off as I eat things. Then I relabeled the pantry jars with masking tape. Rice, lentils, oats, the three vinegars. It took an hour and a half. It's not glamorous, but I think this is how the takeout problem actually gets solved: not with willpower, but with a list on a freezer door.
entries.favorite: The list on the freezer door
entries.highlight: Organized the freezer and pantry and taped up an inventory list to support planned freezer-meal nights.

entries.title: Annual review: senior, and a nudge
entries.body: Annual review today, over video because I was working from home. I was much less nervous than last year. I didn't skip breakfast, at least. Dana started with the good news: a five percent raise and a title change to senior product designer. Senior. She went through the year: empty states, the all-hands, the hiring, Chloe, the sprint planning format, which apparently three other teams are now using. Then her feedback, which was the same as last year, but bigger. She wants me to take on more ownership this year, not just of a project, but of a direction. She brought up onboarding. She said, the lead is still open, and the people who get those things are the people who make a clear case. I said, I'm definitely interested. She said, okay. Afterward I realized that was a hint again. Not an ask. Still working on that.
entries.highlight: Got a raise and promotion to senior product designer, with feedback from Dana to take more ownership and make a case for the onboarding lead.

entries.title: WFH day around the review
entries.body: The rest of the review day, working from home. I did two loads of laundry between calls, mostly to have something to do with my hands before the review at 2. Then I took a real lunch break and walked to the bakery by the lake. It was 22 degrees and the lake was frozen at the edges, with chunks of ice piled up like broken glass. I got the spinach and feta pastry, the same one from my first WFH day in September. After the review, I sat at my desk by the window and wrote down everything Dana said before I forgot it. Then I opened the onboarding thoughts document, which is now nineteen pages, and added a new section at the top: why me. I wrote three sentences and deleted two of them. It's hard to write about yourself. But that section is the clear case Dana was talking about. I need to finish it.
entries.highlight: Worked from home on review day, took a real lunch break by the frozen lake, and started writing a case to lead onboarding.

entries.title: The raise goes to the cushion
entries.body: Paid the bills, or checked the autopay, which is my monthly ritual now. Then I did the same thing I did last year with the raise: before I can get used to the extra money, it gets moved. This year, though, it's not a moving fund. It's the emergency fund. I increased the automatic transfer by $180 a month. That puts me on track to hit three months of expenses by November, instead of next spring. I also downgraded a music app I'd bumped to premium for one road trip, $5 a month. The leaks are getting very small now. That's how I know the boat's in good shape. I'm thinking about last February, when the moving fund was $340 and felt like a fantasy. Now the fantasy has light and a kitchen window. Next fantasy: not panicking if something breaks.
entries.favorite: The leaks are getting very small
entries.highlight: Directed the new raise into the emergency fund, putting it on track to reach three months of expenses by November.

entries.title: Week one cross-training on the bike
entries.body: Did a spin class after work at the new gym, which is part of the race training plan. The plan has three runs a week and one cross-training day, and spin counts. The instructor here is a cheerful guy named Omar who wears a headband and plays nothing but 80s music. He's very different from Tamsin, who would have made me do three extra climbs by now. My legs are already grumbling, because I also did the first two runs of the training plan this week: twenty minutes on the treadmill each, easy pace. My legs had more in them than I expected after a month off. The slump isn't over, I don't think, but I can see the edge of it. Alex texted me after their first training run and said, why do people do this. I sent back a picture of the index card on my fridge.
entries.highlight: Took a spin class as cross-training in the first week of 5K race training and felt stronger than expected.

entries.title: Nineteen pages into two
entries.body: Took the whole morning for the onboarding document, phone in a drawer, Slack closed. My goal was to take the nineteen pages of onboarding thoughts and turn them into something a busy person would actually read. I got it down to two pages. Page one is the problem: new users drop off in the first week, the flow is seven steps that should be three, and our biggest customer said so on that December call. Page two is a plan: research in the spring, design in the summer, launch in the fall. And at the bottom, the why me section, which I finally finished. It just says: I've done this kind of work before, I know the data, and I want to lead it. It was weirdly hard to write the last four words. I haven't sent it to anyone yet. But I have a draft.
entries.favorite: Writing I want to lead it
entries.highlight: Condensed nineteen pages of onboarding notes into a two-page plan, including a statement that they want to lead it.

entries.title: Elena and the 4.0 bug list
entries.body: Had a 1:1 with Elena about bug triage for the 4.0 release, which is the big platform update everyone is working on this year. It's supposed to ship in the summer, and the design bug list is already at forty. Elena is the product manager on it and she's very organized, the kind of person who color codes her calendar. She gave me some useful feedback: my bug write-ups are good, but I'm writing them all myself, and she said, you have Chloe and Tomas, why aren't they writing half of these? I didn't have a great answer. I think it's because I like knowing everything is right. But Elena's point is that I'm the bottleneck. That stung a little. She's not wrong, though. I went back to my desk and assigned eight bugs to Chloe and seven to Tomas. My stomach hurt doing it. Then it was fine.
entries.highlight: Got feedback from PM Elena that they're a bottleneck on bug write-ups and delegated half to teammates.

entries.title: Gait analysis at the running store
entries.body: Saturday errands. First the running store by the lake, because the shoes I've been running in since last spring have a hole in the toe and are basically flat. I've never been to a real running store. They put me on a treadmill and filmed my feet, which is called a gait analysis and is mostly embarrassing. The guy, whose name was Jules, showed me a slow motion video of my left foot rolling inward like it's trying to escape. He picked out three pairs and I jogged up and down the sidewalk in each one in the cold. Got the second pair. $135, more than I've ever spent on shoes, but I'm treating it as race equipment. Then the library to pick up a book on hold, and the post office for stamps. Three stops, and the receipt from the first one still stings a little. My feet already feel more expensive.
entries.favorite: My left foot trying to escape
entries.highlight: Got fitted for proper running shoes with a gait analysis as part of 5K race training.

entries.title: Taco night in the Dutch oven
entries.body: Made tacos for dinner tonight, with carnitas, pork shoulder slow cooked in the Dutch oven for three hours with orange, garlic, cumin, and oregano, then shredded and crisped in the cast iron. Both of the pans my parents gave me, working together. I like to think of them as a team now. While it cooked, I listened to a podcast about a woman who rowed across the Atlantic alone, which made my training runs feel very manageable. I made a quick pickled red onion, which I learned from Priya, and a lime crema. It turned out great. Frankly, restaurant great. I invited Priya over, since she was home, and she had three tacos and said, you know you used to drink soup out of a mug, right? I told her that story once and now everyone knows it. There's enough left for two lunches and a freezer bag.
entries.favorite: Both pans working as a team
entries.highlight: Slow-cooked carnitas tacos using both pans from their parents and shared them with neighbor Priya.

entries.title: Missed run, not a spiral
entries.body: Skipped the Friday training run and went to bed at 9:30. Week three of the plan, and this is the first run I've missed. The reason was very specific: my left shin has been aching since Wednesday's run, right where Jules said my foot rolls in. I looked it up and the internet said a missed run is fine and running through shin pain is not. So I iced it, stretched, and went to bed. The thing I'm proud of isn't the skipping. It's how I feel about it. In the fall, one missed swim turned into a missed week, and then a missed month. Tonight it's just one missed run. I already moved it to Sunday in the training app. The plan has room for this. I'm learning to let it bend instead of break.
entries.highlight: Skipped one training run to rest a sore shin and rescheduled it, without letting it turn into a longer slump.

entries.title: Kale and walnut pesto, too salty
entries.body: Tried a new recipe today: winter pesto, with kale and walnuts instead of basil and pine nuts, since Priya's basil is all indoors and looking sad. I blanched the kale, toasted the walnuts, and blended it all with garlic, lemon, olive oil, and parmesan. The problem was the parmesan. I used the expensive block from January, which is saltier than the cheap kind, and I added salt on top of it. Too much salt. I seem to do this once a season. I fixed it a little with more lemon and a handful of extra kale, and it was good enough on pasta with white beans. Listened to a podcast about the history of salt, which felt like the universe laughing at me. Will definitely make it again, with half the salt. I wrote the adjustment in pen on the recipe, next to my white chili note from October.
entries.highlight: Tried a winter kale and walnut pesto that came out too salty and noted the fix for next time.

entries.title: Sunday swim with Bev, shin healed
entries.body: Went for a swim Sunday morning instead of my usual makeup run, to give the shin one more day. It feels much better. I can walk down stairs without wincing. The pool at 8am on a Sunday is mostly retirees and serious triathletes, and Bev, in the flowered cap, who told me she's seventy-three and has been swimming every day since her husband died in 2015. She said the water is where she does her thinking. I thought about that for my whole swim. Thirty-six laps, sets of six, like October. My swimming came right back, which I didn't expect after the slump. My head stayed clear all day. The weird thing is how much I like this pool, and the people in it, who I only know by their swim caps and their lanes. I think Sunday mornings are going to be a Bev thing now.
entries.favorite: Bev saying the water is where she thinks
entries.highlight: Swam on a Sunday morning to rest a healing shin and had a meaningful conversation with fellow swimmer Bev.

entries.title: Nico says I'm talking fast again
entries.body: Haircut on my lunch break with Nico. It's still cold, but I went short anyway, since the race is in eight weeks and I don't want hair in my face. Nico asked how winter was, picking up right where we left off in January. I told him about the race, the running store, the sprint planning thing, the two page document. He stopped cutting and pointed the scissors at me in the mirror and said, you're talking fast again. Winter was for planning, spring is for doing. He was very proud of his grandfather's saying, which I'm now almost sure he made up. $40. I walked back to the office and ate lunch outside on the bench in the plaza, in my coat, for the first time this year. That's lunch away from my desk two days this week. One more and I hit my goal.
entries.favorite: Nico pointing the scissors at me
entries.highlight: Got a lunch-break haircut, and the barber noticed they seemed energized again, compared to January.

entries.title: Alex asked, Robin said yes
entries.body: Alex proposed to Robin on Saturday, at the little restaurant up north with the view of the waterfall, like Alex planned back in November. I've been holding this secret for four months. Alex called me Sunday night at 9:30 and the first thing they said was, I'm allowed to talk now. Robin said yes before Alex even finished the question, apparently, and then they both cried, and then the waiter brought them free dessert. Robin got the second ring, the one we both liked. Then Alex said the thing that made me sit down on the kitchen floor: we want you in the wedding party. You and Sam. I said yes before Alex finished the question, too. The wedding is going to be next spring. I'm writing this the next day and I'm still smiling. I think about the July coffee, Alex saying Robin is it. It was.
entries.highlight: Alex got engaged to Robin and asked Jordan and Sam to be in the wedding party.

entries.title: The 4.0 design review deck, late
entries.body: Stayed late to finish the slide deck for the 4.0 design review, which is tomorrow morning with the whole leadership team. I got it in at 7:45. Ate lunch at my desk again, which breaks my streak of three outdoor lunches last week. The deck covers the new navigation, the settings changes, and the design system updates, and I made a point of putting Chloe's and Tomas's names on the slides they designed. Last year I learned what it's like to watch someone else get credit for your work. I'm not going to do that to anyone. Ordered pad thai, of course. Marcus was also there late, debugging something, and we ate together in the empty kitchen, like the week before Christmas in 2024. He told me his daughter is learning the trumpet. I told him about Gerald. He said, never let them meet.
entries.highlight: Stayed late to finish the 4.0 design review deck and made sure teammates were credited on their slides.

entries.title: Old running shoes to the recycling bin
entries.body: This morning before work, I did a quick drop-off: the old running shoes with the hole in the toe, plus a bag of worn-out workout shirts, to the shoe and textile recycling bin outside the running store. Jules was opening up and waved at me. I told him the new shoes are working, and the shin pain is gone, and he said, told you, your left foot just needed support, like everyone. I think about that sentence more than I should. Those old shoes ran two miles nonstop in June and carried me around my parents' block in December. It felt a little silly to say goodbye to shoes, but I did, quietly, before dropping them in. Then the 8:05, which was on time for once, and I got a seat. The hallway closet has a lot more room now. Crossed one big thing off the list.
entries.highlight: Recycled worn-out running shoes and old workout clothes at the running store before work.

entries.title: Thirty minutes nonstop, first since June
entries.body: Week five of the race training plan. Tonight's run was thirty minutes without stopping, after work, on the lake path, since it was 51 degrees and still light at 6:30, thanks to daylight saving. I haven't run thirty minutes nonstop since the two mile day last June. It was hard in the middle, around minute eighteen, when my lungs started burning and my brain started listing reasons to stop. But I kept going. I passed the lighthouse at the end of the pier and turned around, and the sun was setting orange over the water, and I made it. Thirty minutes. About 2.3 miles. That's more than I've ever run. My calves feel like two clenched fists right now. I'm going to sleep like a rock tonight. I texted Alex, who said, show off, and then, proud of you.
entries.highlight: Ran thirty minutes without stopping for the first time since last June, covering about 2.3 miles.

entries.title: Engagement brunch, then the museum
entries.body: Celebrated the engagement with Alex and Robin today. We did brunch at a diner near their place, and then Robin wanted to see the new photography exhibit at the art museum, so we went there after. Sam came too. Robin showed off the ring about forty times, and every time, Alex looked at Robin like they'd won something. The exhibit was all black and white photos of weddings from the last hundred years, which Robin swears was a coincidence. My favorite was a couple from the 1940s laughing in the rain under a newspaper. We spent way too long in the gift shop, and I bought Alex and Robin a little frame for an engagement photo. The new exhibit was worth it. Sam and I started a group chat for wedding party stuff called The Index Cards, after our trivia team. Alex hates it. That's the point.
entries.favorite: The couple laughing in the rain
entries.highlight: Celebrated Alex and Robin's engagement with brunch and a museum visit with Sam.

entries.title: Rest day, by the plan
entries.body: No workout today, and lights out by 9:45. But this is a planned rest day, not a slump day, and I want to write down the difference because I didn't understand it a year ago. A planned rest day is part of the work. A slump day is when the work stops. Last April, the running plan's rest days confused me, like they were cheating. Now I get it. My legs are recovering from the thirty-minute run and the long weekend, and the tiredness feels normal and healthy, not heavy. I spent the evening making a big pot of soup, stretching on the floor, and reading the book I picked up from the library. Priya texted from her shift to say the hospital cafeteria was serving green Jell-O for St. Patrick's Day. I'm aiming for nine hours.
entries.highlight: Took a planned rest day during race training and reflected on the difference between rest and a slump.

entries.title: Quarterly metrics, with help this time
entries.body: Stayed late to finish the quarterly metrics before the deadline. I ordered takeout to my desk, and got it in at 7:45. This one was rough because the 4.0 release work has been eating all my focus mornings, so I couldn't do my usual quarterly metrics morning. The tradition broke. But here's what was different: I asked Chloe to pull the empty states numbers and Tomas to do the charts. I just wrote the story around them. A year ago I would have done every piece myself and stayed until 10. With help, it was 7:45. Elena's bottleneck comment from February keeps echoing. I'm learning that delegating feels worse in the moment and better at 7:45. The train home was mostly empty, and I sat by the window and watched the lights on the lake. I ate a cookie Chloe left on my desk with a sticky note that said, for the deadline.
entries.highlight: Finished the quarterly metrics late but faster than usual by delegating parts to Chloe and Tomas.

entries.title: Omar's spin class at 6:30am
entries.body: Did spin before work, Omar's 6:30am class, the cross-training day for race week six. I thought morning spin would be quieter than evening spin, but Omar is somehow even more cheerful at 6:30am. He played a whole song from a movie about dancing and made us stand up for the chorus. I was more awake than usual all morning. My legs feel different this spring. Stronger, more solid. On the stairs at the train station, I don't need the railing anymore. I noticed that last week, and I keep noticing it. I hadn't even realized I was using it before. It's like the strength showed up without telling me. I made the 8:05 with time to spare, and spent the ride reviewing Tomas's navigation designs on my phone, which are very good, and which I said so about in writing.
entries.highlight: Took an early spin class as cross-training and noticed their legs have gotten noticeably stronger this spring.

entries.title: Red lentil coconut soup
entries.body: Thursday is usually a freezer night, but the freezer list on the door is down to two crossed-off boxes and one chili, so I made fresh soup instead, to restock. Red lentil soup with coconut milk, ginger, garlic, turmeric, a can of tomatoes, and a big handful of spinach at the end, with lime. It's a different soup from the regular lentil one, faster, since red lentils break down in twenty minutes. My podcast tonight was about the people who name paint colors, which was surprisingly gripping. It came out creamy and bright and a little spicy. I made enough for two lunches and four freezer portions, and wrote them on the freezer list. Then I sat by the window and watched it get dark at 7:15, which is so much later than December. The light is coming back, and so am I, I think.
entries.highlight: Made a red lentil coconut soup to restock the freezer and noticed the longer evenings returning.

entries.title: Washing the big windows
entries.body: Spent the morning washing all the windows, inside and out, as far as I could safely reach from the inside. Last April I washed the windows in the old apartment for the first time ever, and it was so embarrassing how much brighter it got. These windows were already bright, and I wash them now every season, because I learned that lesson. It's the two big west windows in the living room and the little one over the kitchen sink. Took about an hour with vinegar and newspaper, Mom's trick. Then I swept the hallway and wiped down the baseboards and put away the winter blanket. The apartment feels so much better, and so much lighter, which is the same thing. The street side windows are clear enough that I forget they're there. In the afternoon, the light came across the floor, and I lay down in it with a book, like a cat.
entries.highlight: Washed the apartment windows for spring, a habit started after the dirty windows in the old apartment.

entries.title: Taxes filed in March, from a folder
entries.body: Did the monthly bill check and then filed my taxes, in March, for the first time in my life. Last February, my tax documents lived in a shoebox under my bed. This year they live in a folder labeled taxes, and I added each document as it came in. It took fifty minutes total. I'm getting a refund of about $700, and I already know where it's going: half to the emergency fund and half to a new account I opened tonight, called wedding, for Alex and Robin's wedding next spring. Being in the wedding party means a suit, travel, a gift, and probably a weekend somewhere. I'd rather save for it now than panic about it later. And I dropped the premium cloud storage, since I finally cleaned up my photos. I'm very proud of my folder. That might be the most boring sentence I've ever said.
entries.highlight: Filed taxes early from an organized folder and split the refund between the emergency fund and a new wedding fund.

entries.title: Negotiating the research vendor
entries.body: Had a 1:1 with Elena about the vendor contract for a user research tool. We need it for the 4.0 release, to test the new navigation with real users, and the vendor sent us a quote that was very high. Elena asked me to handle the negotiation, since I'm the one who'll use the tool the most. I've never negotiated anything at work. Elena gave me some useful feedback: know your walk-away number, ask for what you want, then stop talking. That's the same advice Alex used to ask for the promotion. Everybody seems to know this but me. I emailed the vendor tonight, asked for a twenty percent discount and a longer trial, and then I stopped typing. It's harder than it sounds. I wanted to add three more sentences explaining myself. I didn't.
entries.highlight: Took on negotiating a research vendor contract for the first time, using Elena's advice to ask clearly and stop talking.

entries.title: Long standup, outdoor lunch anyway
entries.body: Started with standup, which ran long, twenty-five minutes for what should be ten, because two people argued about a deadline. Then back-to-back calls until lunch. But I protected lunch. I put a block on my calendar called lunch, outside, and actually went outside, to the bench in the plaza, with leftover red lentil soup in a thermos. It was 56 degrees and windy, and a pigeon watched me eat the whole time. That's my third outdoor lunch this week, so I hit my goal from the new year card for the first time. Three days away from my desk. It sounds small, but I've been trying to do this for over a year. The afternoon was better. I was less cranky in the 3pm meeting. Also, the vendor wrote back: fifteen percent off and a longer trial. Not twenty. But not nothing. Elena said, nice.
entries.highlight: Protected their lunch break despite a busy day and hit the goal of three lunches away from the desk in one week.

entries.title: Soup across the hall for Priya
entries.body: Priya texted me this afternoon that she has the flu and has been in bed for two days. So tonight I made lentil soup, the regular kind, the good version from January, in the Dutch oven, and brought her a big container, plus a sleeve of crackers and some ginger ale from the corner store. I left it all on her doorknob in a bag, like she did with the basil in September, with a note that said, eat it before it dies. She texted back a crying laughing face and then, an hour later, it's perfect. Then I ate my own bowl by the window. It was good, of course, because at this point lentil soup is just a thing I know how to make. It's nice to be the neighbor who brings soup instead of only the one who borrows basil.
entries.favorite: Using Priya's own note on her
entries.highlight: Made lentil soup for neighbor Priya while she had the flu and left it at her door with a callback note.

entries.title: April Fools and the 4.0 schedule slip
entries.body: The 8:05 was late, which I briefly hoped was an April Fools joke. At the office, someone had replaced all the kitchen coffee mugs with tiny espresso cups as an April Fools joke, and Marcus was walking around with a cup the size of a thimble, refilling it every two minutes. The not-funny news: the 4.0 release is slipping. It was supposed to ship in July, and now it's looking like early fall. There are too many dependencies on the backend team. Elena was stressed and so was I. But I noticed something about myself: I wasn't panicking. I was making a list. What design work can move up, what can be cut, who needs to know. A year ago, a slipped deadline would have ruined my week. Now it's a problem with a list. The train home was packed. I stood. I didn't mind.
entries.highlight: Learned the 4.0 release is slipping to fall and noticed they responded calmly with a plan instead of panic.

entries.title: Wedding fund and an old app
entries.body: Checked the bills this morning. All on autopay, all good. Rent, electric, gas, internet. I set up autopay for the new renter's insurance policy, which I finally bought this month after Priya told me about a pipe that burst on the third floor before I moved in. $14 a month, which is nothing compared to replacing everything I own. Then I found a zombie: a fitness app from 2024 that I forgot to delete, which had somehow started charging again. I emailed them and got a refund. Asking works. Then I moved $100 into the wedding fund. It has $450 now. Alex sent the save the date this week, for next May, at a lodge by a lake up north, and the group chat, The Index Cards, has been very active. Sam is already planning toasts. I'm planning a budget.
entries.highlight: Set up renter's insurance, got a refund on a forgotten subscription, and grew the wedding fund after Alex's save-the-date.

entries.title: Onboarding pushed to Q4
entries.body: Made it to the all-hands with a minute to spare, where the CEO announced that because of the 4.0 slip, the onboarding redesign is moving to Q4. The lead will be named in the fall. I sat with that for a while. My first feeling was disappointment, a heavy one, like when the lights go out early in October. The two page document has been sitting in my drafts since February, and I never sent it. I kept waiting for the right moment. Now the moment moved. But on the train home I thought about it differently. If I'm the design lead on 4.0, and it ships well, that's the clearest case I could ever make. It's six months of proof. Marcus messaged me: still yours. I wrote back: still mine. Then I added the date to my calendar: ask Dana, early October.
entries.highlight: Learned the onboarding redesign was pushed to Q4 and decided to use the 4.0 release to build their case to lead it.

entries.title: Emergency fund passes $4,000
entries.body: Monthly budget check-in. Groceries were $226, because I've been cooking from the freezer list and the farmers market starts again soon. Eating out was $141, the second lowest month ever. The freezer nights plan works, which I want to say out loud: Tuesdays and Thursdays basically never have takeout anymore. I moved some money into savings, the tax refund half and the usual transfer, and the emergency fund passed $4,000 this week, $4,120. That's about forty percent of three months. I made a new line on the chart in the spreadsheet, like I did for the moving fund last May, and I'm ahead of it. Ahead. Not catching up. I don't think I've ever been ahead on anything with money. I sat there looking at the chart for a while with my tea. It's a calm feeling. I didn't know money could feel calm.
entries.highlight: Reviewed a strong month's budget, saw the emergency fund pass $4,000, and felt calm and ahead of schedule.

entries.title: Named design lead on 4.0
entries.body: Dana pulled me into a room at 2 today and said she's naming me design lead for the 4.0 release, officially, with Chloe and Tomas reporting to me on it. It's not a management title, but it's the closest thing. I stayed late to finish the kickoff deck for tomorrow, so I could present the new design plan and the new schedule to the whole release team. Got it in at 7:45, with takeout pad thai at my desk, as is tradition. But I did something new: I didn't make the whole deck myself. Chloe did the research timeline slides and Tomas did the navigation slides, and I did the story that ties them together. I took the train home with my head against the window, thinking about the first spec I ever wrote here, which nobody read. This time, people will read it. I'm leading something big.
entries.highlight: Was officially named design lead for the 4.0 release, leading Chloe and Tomas, and prepared the kickoff deck as a team.

entries.title: Taper week nerves
entries.body: Skipped the workout and went to bed at 9:30. It's taper week, the last week before the race on Sunday, which means the training plan says to run less and rest more. I find that extremely stressful. Everything in me wants to do one more long run to prove I can. But the plan says no, so I'm listening. My nerves aren't helping, either. I've been sleeping badly, waking up at 4am thinking about the race, and the 4.0 kickoff, and whether I'll have to walk during the race in front of everyone. Priya told me nurses have a trick for anxious nights: write down what's worrying you, then write down one thing you can actually do about it. So I wrote: worry, walking during the race. Thing I can do: start slow. Then I put the paper on the nightstand and fell asleep.
entries.highlight: Rested during taper week before the 5K race and used Priya's trick of writing down worries to fall asleep.

entries.title: Dad walked around the block, no cane
entries.body: Called Mom on my walk home from the grocery store, the night before the race. She put Dad on speaker. He finished his last physical therapy session on Thursday. Three months, twice a week, with Deshawn. And this morning, he walked around the whole block with Mom, without the cane. He said it slowly, like he was proud of himself but didn't want to admit it. Then he said, so I did my lap, now you do yours tomorrow. I almost cried in the middle of the sidewalk. Mom says the knee isn't perfect, it still aches in the rain, but he can do the stairs to the basement again, which he hasn't done in a year. And she says he's agreed to build the raised garden bed with her in May, as long as I come up to help. I'm going to run tomorrow for both of us.
entries.favorite: Dad saying now you do yours
entries.highlight: Learned Dad finished physical therapy and walked around the block without his cane, the night before Jordan's 5K race.

entries.title: Race day: my first full 5K
entries.body: I ran a 5K. The whole thing, without stopping. The spring race by the lake, 8am start, about four hundred people, a lot of them in costumes for some reason, including a man dressed as a banana. Alex ran too, and we started together near the back, and Alex said go, don't wait for me. I started slow, like I wrote on my worry paper. Mile one felt fine. Mile two, near the lighthouse, felt hard. In mile three, a woman on the sidelines was holding a sign that said, you're doing it, and I was. I crossed the finish line in 34 minutes and 12 seconds. Sam and Priya were at the finish with a sign that said, The Index Card. Alex came in eight minutes later, walking the last part, and swearing. Then I called Dad and told him I did my lap. He said, I know. I could tell.
entries.highlight: Ran a full 5K race without stopping for the first time, finishing in 34:12, completing a goal first set in January 2025.

entries.title: Post-race yoga with Hal
entries.body: Did yoga after work with Hal and his rain sounds, because the training plan said a gentle recovery day. My legs hurt today, which is fair, considering what I asked of them yesterday. My calves feel like they're full of wet sand, and going down the stairs at the train station was a little comic. But I felt strong today in a new way. I keep forgetting and then remembering: I ran a 5K. I keep looking at the medal on the hook by my door, a little cheap medal with a lighthouse on it, and smiling. At the end of class, lying in the dark, I thought about the first index card on my fridge in January 2025, run a 5K, and how it took me sixteen months, one move, one slump, and one new pair of shoes. It's not fast. But it's done. Hal said, notice how far you've come. He meant the class. I didn't.
entries.highlight: Took a gentle recovery yoga class the day after the race and reflected on the 16 months it took to reach the 5K goal.

entries.title: Cod tacos and too much lime salt
entries.body: Cod tacos tonight, a first for me, a crunchy cabbage slaw, and a chipotle crema. The cod was easy, just seasoned and seared in the cast iron, which I'm not afraid of anymore. The problem was the slaw. The recipe said to toss it with lime salt, which is lime zest mixed with salt, and I made a whole quarter cup of it and used way too much. Too much salt, again. I think I have a salt problem. Every season, a new salt mistake. I'm almost proud of my consistency. I rinsed the slaw in a colander, which is a strange thing to do to a salad, and it was fine after that. The crema alone earns these a second chance. I ate three tacos standing at the counter, and then a fourth sitting down, like a civilized person.
entries.highlight: Tried cod tacos with too-salty slaw, rinsed it to save the dish, and planned to make them again.

entries.title: Spring pea pesto, salt measured
entries.body: Tried another new recipe, spring pea pesto, with frozen peas, mint, parmesan, lemon, and a little garlic. After yesterday's slaw, I measured the salt with an actual measuring spoon instead of just pouring, and then I tasted before adding more, and then I didn't add more. It's amazing how much easier cooking is when you taste things before adding salt. A lesson I apparently need to learn every three months. It came out bright green and sweet and fresh. I tossed it with pasta and some ricotta and ate it by the open window, because it was 64 degrees and the trees on my street are finally green. Going on the rotation list. Not too salty. I'm noting the date. I also made extra for tomorrow's lunch, which I'm going to eat outside, on the bench, because it's May tomorrow, and that's the rule now.
entries.highlight: Made a spring pea pesto, carefully measured the salt this time, and enjoyed it by the open window.

entries.title: Chloe asks to run the vendor
entries.body: Had a 1:1 with Chloe, our weekly mentoring session, which we've done for almost a year now. She asked if she could take over the research vendor relationship for 4.0. Set up the studies, manage the contract, run the sessions. She's done her homework: she had a list of reasons, she asked clearly, and then she stopped talking. Just like I learned from Elena. Just like Alex did. I recognized it immediately. I had a moment where I wanted to keep it, since I negotiated that contract and I like it. But this is exactly what Elena was talking about, and what Dana keeps telling me. So I said yes. The plan took five minutes: she takes it over next week, and I'm her backup. After she left, I sat there for a minute. A year ago, she was asking me how to know when a design is done. Now she's asking to own things.
entries.highlight: Agreed to let mentee Chloe take over the research vendor relationship after she asked clearly for the responsibility.

entries.title: Morning yoga and the after-goal question
entries.body: Did the 6:15 yoga class before work for the first time since the race. I was stiff and slow. My calves are mostly back to normal, but my hips are tight from all the training. The whole class, I was thinking about a question I didn't expect to have: what now? For sixteen months, the 5K was the goal on the fridge. Now it's done, and part of me wants to stop, like I've earned it. That's how I lost the running last fall. So I made a small decision on the mat: no new big goal yet, just keep the habit. Three workouts a week, any kind. Run, swim, spin, yoga, whatever. No race, no finish line, just showing up. I think I've learned that the goal gets you started and the habit keeps you going. The eye pillow woman was there, by the window, as always. Some things never change.
entries.favorite: The goal starts it, the habit keeps it
entries.highlight: Returned to morning yoga after the race and decided to focus on keeping a three-workouts-a-week habit rather than a new goal.

entries.title: Chicken tinga, salt tasted first
entries.body: New recipe night again: chicken tinga tacos, with shredded chicken simmered in a sauce of tomatoes, chipotle, onion, and garlic. I made the recipe exactly as written, with one change. I didn't add any salt until the very end, and I tasted it three times before adding a single pinch. It was perfect. After the cod taco lime salt situation last week, and the pesto in February, and the white chili in October, I think I have finally learned the lesson. It took me a year and a half. Had an episode about glaciers on while it simmered, which felt right for anything with chipotle in it. Priya came over with homemade pickled onions, which she now makes in batches and gives to the whole building. We ate on my little balcony-sized window ledge, which is not a balcony, but I put two chairs by the open window and it felt like one. Next time I change nothing.
entries.highlight: Made chicken tinga tacos with perfectly measured salt, finally learning from a string of salty-recipe mistakes.

entries.title: Bug triage night, three of us
entries.body: Stayed late to finish bug triage for the 4.0 beta before the deadline. The beta goes to fifty customers next week, and we had thirty-four design bugs still open. Ordered takeout to my desk, but this time for three, because Chloe and Tomas stayed too. Last year, this would have been me alone at 9pm under the motion lights. This year, we split the list into three, put on music, and got it in at 7:45. Tomas found a bug in a screen I designed and was nervous to tell me, and I told him, that's exactly what I want you to do, which I think surprised him. Chloe ordered dessert for everyone with her own money, which I made her expense. Then I sent them both home and took the train alone, tired, but not the old kind of tired. More like the tired you feel after a long relay. A team tired.
entries.favorite: Tomas telling me about my own bug
entries.highlight: Worked late with Chloe and Tomas to clear 4.0 beta design bugs, sharing the load as a team.

entries.title: Sheet swap without the laundromat
entries.body: Did the seasonal sheet swap this morning before work. Flannel off, cotton on. Last May, I did this exact thing and had to haul the flannel sheets to the laundromat on my lunch break. This year, I just threw them in the washer in my own closet, and they were dry and folded before I left for the 8:05. It's been eight months in this apartment and I still feel a little thrill every time I use the washer. I don't think that's going away. Also took out the recycling, which in this building means a trip to the basement, where Gerald was sorting his own recycling and practicing a trumpet piece by humming it. He's playing at a wedding in June. I told him I'm in a wedding next year and he offered his services, which I may pass on to Alex. Summer bed, ready.
entries.highlight: Did the spring sheet swap using the in-unit washer and chatted with neighbor Gerald in the recycling room.

entries.title: Seed packets to Mom, and a cat update
entries.body: Ran errands after work. The post office first, where the line wrapped around the stamp machine, but the cat was awake today, sitting on the scale. I mailed Mom a box of heirloom tomato seeds and a little hand trowel with a wooden handle that I found at the hardware store, a late Mother's Day gift, since I only had time to call her on Sunday. Walt at the hardware store helped me pick the trowel. He said, for a serious gardener? and I said, the most serious, and he went into the back and came out with the good one. Then the pharmacy for my allergy refill, which, a year later, is still good but slow. I read three articles on my phone while I waited. Three stops, three people who know my name. I'm a regular at every place on this route now. That's the thing about staying somewhere. You become part of it.
entries.favorite: Walt bringing out the good trowel
entries.highlight: Mailed Mom heirloom tomato seeds and a quality trowel for Mother's Day and reflected on becoming a regular in the neighborhood.

entries.title: Sheet-pan chicken, the reliable one
entries.body: Meal-prepped lunches for the week this morning: sheet-pan chicken, the same recipe I made back in February 2025, when I was shocked that it only used one pan. Chicken thighs, potatoes, red onion, paprika, olive oil, 425 degrees, forty minutes. This time I doubled it and added a second sheet pan of broccoli and chickpeas, so it's two pans now, but still very easy. Took about an hour and fifteen minutes, including cleanup, with a podcast on. Five lunches, plus two dinners. Good, because this is a very busy week, with the 4.0 beta launching to customers on Tuesday. The thing I've learned is that you need a few recipes you could make half asleep, so the busy weeks don't fall apart. This is one. The lentil soup is another. The stir-fry is the third. I have a rotation now. I'm a person with a rotation.
entries.favorite: Being a person with a rotation
entries.highlight: Meal-prepped a double batch of their reliable sheet-pan chicken to prepare for a busy work week.

entries.title: Annual physical: resting heart rate down
entries.body: Annual physical this morning, at 8, before work. Everything looks normal again, but it's better than normal in a few places. My resting heart rate is down eight beats from last year. My blood pressure is better. My vitamin D is fine now, because I've been eating lunch outside, which the doctor said was a perfectly scientific approach. She asked about exercise, and I told her about the 5K, and she actually put her pen down and said, good for you, that's a big one. Last year when I told her I was running twelve minutes she said that counts, and I could tell she was being nice. This year I could tell she meant it. She said to keep up the exercise and keep sleeping, and to wear sunscreen at lunch. I walked out of the office feeling like I'd gotten a good report card. I've never been this healthy as an adult.
entries.favorite: The doctor putting her pen down
entries.highlight: Had an annual physical showing a lower resting heart rate and better blood pressure, and the doctor praised the 5K.

entries.title: Last quarterly metrics I do alone
entries.body: Beta launch day for 4.0, which went fine, mostly. And the quarterly metrics were due tonight, too, because of course they were. Stayed late to finish them. Ate cold noodles at my desk and finally hit send at 8:20. Ate lunch at my desk again too, which hurts after hitting my outdoor lunch goal most weeks this spring. But this was a launch day, and launch days get an exception. On the train home I made a decision: this is the last quarterly metrics I do by myself. Next quarter, Chloe takes the lead, and I review it. It's a good stretch for her and it frees up a whole morning for me. I keep doing this thing where I delegate, then take it back, then delegate. Elena said I'm a bottleneck, and I fixed it for a while, and then on busy days I go back to doing everything. Writing it down so I remember.
entries.highlight: Stayed late on 4.0 beta launch day to finish quarterly metrics and decided to hand future metrics to Chloe.

entries.title: Dad knelt in the garden
entries.body: Took the early train to my parents' for the weekend to help build Mom's raised garden bed. The plan fell apart immediately, because the lumber delivery didn't come, and the company said Tuesday. Mom was furious for about ten minutes and then said, fine, we'll plant the regular garden. So we did. Tomatoes from her nursery, peppers, beans, and the heirloom tomato seeds I mailed her. Here's what got me: Dad knelt down in the garden to plant a row of beans. On both knees. In the dirt. Last Mother's Day he sat in a lawn chair on the edge of the yard because he couldn't kneel at all. Mom and I looked at each other and didn't say anything, because we both knew he'd get embarrassed. He planted the whole row. The raised bed is postponed until next spring, Mom says. I promised I'd help. Train home at 6, covered in dirt again.
entries.favorite: Dad on both knees in the dirt
entries.highlight: Helped plant their parents' garden when the raised bed lumber didn't arrive, and saw Dad kneel in the garden after physical therapy.

entries.title: Sunday list, eighty-four dollars
entries.body: Got back from my parents' late last night, so I did the grocery run this morning at 8:15. Stuck to the list, which is no longer a thing I need to celebrate, it's just how I shop. Chicken thighs, onions, salmon, tomatoes, a big bag of lentils, cucumbers, feta, lemons, eggs, oat milk, and coffee. $84. Mom sent me home with a bag of asparagus from her garden, so I didn't need to buy vegetables for the first half of the week. The store has the first local strawberries, but they were $7 a box, so I'm waiting for the farmers market. I've learned this year that the farmers market and the grocery store each have a job. The grocery store is for staples, and the market is for things that taste like a season. That's either very wise or very boring. Probably both.
entries.highlight: Did the Sunday grocery run for $84 and reflected on using the grocery store for staples and the market for seasonal food.

entries.title: Lentil salad instead of soup
entries.body: It's too warm for lentil soup, 78 degrees today, so I made a lentil salad instead, which is basically the summer version. Cooked the green lentils until they were just tender, not mushy, then tossed them with cucumber, tomatoes, red onion, feta, parsley, lemon, and olive oil. And then I tasted it before adding salt, which is my new religion. Listened to a long podcast about the history of the lighthouse service, because I'm apparently obsessed with lighthouses now, since the race medal. The salad was really fresh and filling. Enough leftovers for two days of lunches, or three, if I'm careful. I'm going to eat them outside on the bench, obviously. I keep coming back to lentils. I made the watery soup in November 2024 because I thought it was impossible to mess up, and I was wrong. Now I can do lentils four ways.
entries.highlight: Made a summer lentil salad as a warm-weather version of their usual lentil soup.

entries.title: Memorial Day picnic and Sam's final round
entries.body: Memorial Day picnic by the lake with Sam, Alex, Robin, and Priya. We got a picnic table near the beach at 11 and stayed until the sun went down. I brought the lentil salad and a rhubarb crumble, Mrs. Okafor's recipe from last year, with plenty of sugar this time. Alex and Robin brought a cooler of drinks and a binder of wedding venue options, which they showed us whether we wanted to see it or not. Then Sam told us the news: they have a final round interview at a climate organization, for the communications job Sam has wanted all along. Sam's been searching for eight months. Two near misses, a lot of cover letters, a lot of patience. We all cheered so loudly that a family at the next table looked over. Then Sam and I retold the pivot couch story, again, and Priya, who had never heard it, laughed until she nearly fell off the bench.
entries.favorite: Cheering for Sam at the picnic table
entries.highlight: Spent Memorial Day at a lakeside picnic with friends and celebrated Sam reaching a final-round interview after eight months of searching.

entries.title: Summer cut and Nico's question
entries.body: Haircut on my lunch break with Nico. Went a little shorter than usual for summer, which is now my seasonal tradition, apparently. Nico asked about the race. I told him I finished in 34 minutes, and he put the scissors down and shook my hand, which got the whole shop looking at us. Then he asked a question that's stuck with me all day: what's next? Everyone keeps asking me that. I told him I'm not chasing anything for a while. I'm just trying to keep the good habits I built. He nodded and said that's harder than chasing. I think he's right. It's easy to be motivated by a finish line. It's harder to keep going when there isn't one. $42. I tipped extra again. Then I ate my lentil salad on the bench and watched the pigeons fight over a pretzel.
entries.favorite: Nico shaking my hand in the shop
entries.highlight: Got a summer haircut, and the barber celebrated the 5K and noted that keeping habits is harder than chasing goals.

entries.title: Sent the team home, did it myself
entries.body: Stayed late to finish the 4.0 navigation spec before the engineering deadline Monday. Ordered a sandwich to my desk and finished at 8:10. Here's the part I'm not proud of. At 5:30, Chloe and Tomas offered to stay, and I said no, go home, it's Friday, I've got it. It felt generous. But on the train home, I realized it wasn't generous, it was the old habit. I didn't want to explain the spec, so I just did it. Two weeks ago, I promised myself I'd stop doing this. And now I've done it again, on a Friday, in a nice way, which is the sneakiest way. Tomas would have been great at the edge case section. Chloe has been asking for more spec work. I took that from them, kind of. So I wrote them both a message for Monday: next spec, you two draft, I'll review. Pressing send before I can change my mind.
entries.highlight: Stayed late alone on a spec after sending teammates home, then recognized it as an old habit and committed to delegating the next one.

entries.title: May was a celebration month again
entries.body: Monthly budget check-in for May. Eating out was $232, which is too much, and I know exactly why, and I'm not upset. The race celebration dinner, the engagement brunch's sequel, two nights out with Sam to prep for the final round, and the picnic. Every one of them, I could name in one sentence, which was my rule from last July: if you can name what you're celebrating, it counts. They all counted. Groceries were $219. I moved some money into savings: $300 to the emergency fund, which is at $5,850, more than half of the goal, and $100 to the wedding fund. I also looked back at June last year, when I paid the deposit for this apartment and nearly emptied the moving fund. One year ago I had almost nothing, and was scared. Now I have half a cushion, and I'm not scared of a celebration month. Progress isn't always a lower number.
entries.favorite: Progress isn't always a lower number
entries.highlight: Reviewed May's celebration-heavy spending calmly and saw the emergency fund pass half of its goal.

entries.title: Donation bag from the summer swap
entries.body: Did the summer clothes swap tonight. Winter sweaters into the bins under the bed, summer shirts into the closet.
