While doing it, I filled a donation bag with everything I didn't wear last summer, which turned out to be a lot. Three shirts, two pairs of shorts I never liked, a pair of sandals that hurt. I've gotten better at this. In the old apartment, donation bags would sit in my hallway for a month, then move to my trunk for another month. Tonight I filled the bag, put it in my car, and drove it to the donation center on the way to the gym. Twenty minutes. Done. The closet looks huge now, or at least I can see the back wall. There was a bit of a moment with the lobster hat. I kept it. Some things are not for donating. I'm going to wear it to Alex's bachelor party.
entries.favorite: Keeping the lobster hat for Alex's party
entries.highlight: Did the seasonal clothes swap and dropped off a donation bag the same night, unlike the old habit of letting bags sit for weeks.

entries.title: Ravi's lemongrass stir-fry
entries.body: Made something new tonight: a lemongrass chicken stir-fry that Ravi's dad makes, which Ravi wrote down for me on the back of a meeting agenda. Lemongrass, garlic, shallots, nam pla, a little sugar, chili, and chicken thighs, with green beans and basil at the end. I've never cooked with lemongrass. You have to bash it with the back of a knife first, which was extremely satisfying after a long Wednesday. The nam pla is salty, so I added it a little at a time and tasted, which is my new religion. Still came out a tiny bit too salty, because I forgot the nam pla counts as salt. Note for round two: less nam pla. The apartment smelled so good that I'm already planning it. The podcast this time was a guy who walked across the whole country, which made my Wednesday feel short. Sent Ravi a photo. He sent back, Dad says more chili.
entries.highlight: Tried Ravi's father's lemongrass chicken stir-fry recipe, cooking with lemongrass for the first time.

entries.title: Shopped around for car insurance
entries.body: Checked the bills this morning. Autopay did its thing. Then I did something I've been putting off for two years: I shopped around for car insurance. I barely drive the car, and I've been paying the same company since 2021 without ever looking. It took an hour on my lunch break, outside on the bench, with my phone. I found a policy with the same coverage for $210 a year less, mostly because I drive so little now. I called my current company to cancel, and they offered to match it right away. I took the match, because switching felt like a hassle. But it made me think about how much money I left on the table just by never asking. Two years at $210 is $420. Asking works, again. Also dropped a newspaper app I signed up for in March. Small leak, plugged.
entries.highlight: Shopped around for car insurance and got their current insurer to match a quote that saves $210 a year.

entries.title: A year of light, on a bench
entries.body: Spent the afternoon walking by the lake, then sat on a bench near the lighthouse and read for an hour. It's been one year and two days since I got the email that my application was approved, the one I read during a meeting about blank screens. I've been thinking about that. A year ago I didn't know Priya, or Gerald, or Walt, or Bev, or the post office cat. I didn't know this path. I'd never run a 5K. I hadn't hosted a dinner party. I was a little scared all the time, and I'm a lot less scared now. Some of that is the apartment. Most of it is the stuff I did while living in it. The book I was reading was about a woman who moves to a lighthouse to be alone and ends up becoming part of the whole town. A little on the nose, but I loved it. Walked home in the gold light.
entries.highlight: Spent an afternoon reading by the lake and reflected on how much life has changed in the year since moving.

entries.title: Renewing the lease at $1,940
entries.body: The lease renewal letter came this week, and I did the budget check-in tonight with it next to my laptop. Rent is going up to $1,940 in September, $50 more. Last year, the renewal letter at the old place made me decide to leave. This year it's a very different feeling. I want to stay. I love it here. So I ran the numbers: $50 more a month is $600 a year, and I can absorb that without changing much. Groceries came in under budget again, $211, the lowest ever. I'm going to renew, and I'm going to sign it tomorrow, in daylight. I wrote a short email to the landlord asking if they'd do $1,915 for a two year lease. I was polite and clear, and then I stopped typing. Just like Elena taught me. If they say no, that's fine. But I'm not leaving money on the table without asking anymore.
entries.highlight: Decided to renew the lease despite a $50 increase and asked the landlord for a lower rate on a two-year lease.

entries.title: WFH Wednesday, bakery lunch
entries.body: Worked from home today, at the desk by the west window, which in June gets so hot by 4pm that I have to close the blinds. Did laundry between calls, two loads, and folded them during a meeting with my camera off, a habit I've accepted. The best part: I took a real lunch break and walked to the bakery by the lake. Spinach and feta pastry, which I've now ordered probably thirty times. The woman at the counter says, the usual? and I love that. I sat on the bench and watched people sailing. Then I came back and reviewed the first spec Chloe and Tomas drafted together, the one I promised them after the Friday I did it all myself. It's good. It's different from how I'd write it. The edge cases are better. The intro is too long. I left six comments and none of them were rewrite this. That's growth, for both of us.
entries.highlight: Worked from home, took a real lunch break by the lake, and reviewed a spec drafted by Chloe and Tomas without taking it over.

entries.title: Elena and the bug list at zero
entries.body: Had a 1:1 with Elena about bug triage for 4.0. The design bug list, which was at forty in February, is at four. Four. Elena brought a printout, which she never does, and circled the number. She said, you stopped being the bottleneck. I told her the honest version: I stopped being the bottleneck most of the time, but I still have Fridays where I sneak back into it. She laughed and said everyone does. We mapped out the last four bugs and the summer schedule: code freeze in August, launch in late September, if the backend team doesn't slip again. Then I logged off at 5:30 sharp and went to the gym, where I swam thirty-eight laps, nine in a row without stopping. Bev said I'm finally not splashing. High praise from Bev. It's the little things this week.
entries.highlight: Met with Elena, who celebrated the 4.0 design bug list dropping from forty to four, then went for a strong swim.

entries.title: Strawberries with Priya at the market
entries.body: Walked to the farmers market this morning, the big outdoor one in the park near the lake. It's my second summer here, and I know the vendors now: the honey guy, the bread woman, the egg farm with the named chickens, which have their own little photo board. Bought bananas, oat milk, a loaf of sourdough, and the first real strawberries, which were the reason I waited two weeks instead of buying the $7 grocery store ones. $36 total. Ran into Priya by the flower stand. She'd just gotten off a night shift and was still in scrubs, buying basil seedlings for her balcony. We got iced coffees and walked home together, splitting the strawberries out of the box and getting sticky red fingers. She said, remember when you didn't know where the recycling was? It was nine months ago. It feels like forever. She's my closest friend in the neighborhood now.
entries.highlight: Visited the summer farmers market, ran into Priya, and shared strawberries on the walk home.

entries.title: Pricing the wedding party
entries.body: Mid-month budget check-in, mostly to look at the wedding fund. Groceries are at $98 halfway through the month. The landlord said yes to the two year lease at $1,915, by the way. I asked, I stopped typing, and they said yes. That's $300 a year saved because I sent a four sentence email. Then I sat down with the wedding party math. Alex and Robin's wedding is next May at a lodge up north. I'll need a suit or something nice, maybe $300. Travel and two nights at the lodge, maybe $450. A gift, $150. The bachelor party in the spring, probably a weekend, maybe $300. That's $1,200. The wedding fund has $650. If I add $100 a month, I'll have it by March, with room to spare. I like knowing this now, a year early, instead of finding out with a credit card statement.
entries.highlight: Got approved for a lower two-year lease rate after asking, and planned the full budget for being in Alex's wedding party.

entries.title: Holiday rest in the heat
entries.body: Day off for the holiday, and it was 93 degrees by noon. I'd planned a run, but the heat advisory said to avoid outdoor exercise after 10am, and I didn't wake up until 9:15. So I skipped the workout, and I'll be in bed by 9:45 tonight. The heat made the decision for me, and frankly, I needed it. I've done three workouts a week for seven weeks since the race, which is the longest stretch of consistency I've ever had. Running, swimming, Omar's spin, Hal's yoga. I wasn't going to break the streak for nothing, but a heat advisory is not nothing. I spent the day in the apartment with the blinds closed and the fan on, reading, and I made a cold noodle salad for dinner. I think this is what it looks like when rest is a choice, not a collapse. I can tell the difference now. That's new.
entries.favorite: Rest as a choice, not a collapse
entries.highlight: Took a rest day during a holiday heat advisory, seven weeks into a consistent three-workouts-a-week habit.

entries.title: Father's Day: Dad stands on both legs
entries.body: Took the train up for Father's Day. Dad wanted burgers on the grill again, like last year, and he grilled them himself again, but this time standing on both legs. Last year, he stood on one leg like a flamingo the whole time and Mom and I kept exchanging looks. This year, there was nothing to look at. He just stood there and flipped burgers and talked about baseball. I brought him a new grill apron that says the knee is fine, stop asking, which I had printed, and he laughed so hard he had to sit down, which kind of defeated the point. After lunch, Dad and I went for a walk around the block together, his idea. Slowly, but no cane. He told me Deshawn says he can start walking a mile a day. He asked how far I run now. I said about three miles. He said, maybe I'll catch up. I believe him.
entries.favorite: The apron that says the knee is fine
entries.highlight: Spent Father's Day with Dad, who grilled standing on both legs and went for a walk without a cane, compared to last year.

entries.title: Friday morning reset
entries.body: Spent the morning, before my 10am meeting, doing what I've started calling the Friday reset. Change the sheets, take out the recycling, wipe the kitchen, water the plants, and do one small fix-it thing. This week's fix-it thing was a cabinet door in the kitchen that's been hanging crooked since I moved in. Walt at the hardware store told me the hinge just needs a tightening, and he was right. One screwdriver, two minutes. I have no idea why I waited ten months. Probably the same reason I waited two years to set up autopay for electricity back in 2024. Some tasks are only hard until you start them. The plant cutting from Mrs. Okafor, the one in the jam jar from moving day, has finally grown big enough to put in a real pot, so I did that too. It's thriving. The apartment feels so much better, every Friday now.
entries.highlight: Did a Friday morning home reset, finally fixed a crooked cabinet door, and repotted a plant from a former neighbor.

entries.title: Hal's summer yoga, and a thought
entries.body: Did yoga after work with Hal, who has switched from rain sounds to ocean sounds for the summer. It's a whole production. My legs are going to hurt tomorrow, because we did a long series of lunges again, which Hal described, once again, as gentle. I was struck during the last pose by how different my body feels than when I started yoga in January 2025, in that crowded resolution class, when my hamstrings were guitar strings. I can touch my toes now. My shoulders don't sit up by my ears all day anymore. I don't get the 10am headache. I didn't notice any of this happening. It just happened, a little at a time, one class after another. I think that's how most things change. Not with a big moment like the race, but with a lot of small ones nobody sees. I lay there listening to the fake ocean, and felt good about that.
entries.highlight: Took an evening yoga class and reflected on how much their body has changed since starting in January 2025.

entries.title: Backup duty on a holiday Friday
entries.body: The office was closed today for the holiday, but the research vendor contract renewal was due by end of day, and Chloe, who owns the vendor now, was on a plane to her sister's wedding. So I did my job as her backup. That's the deal we made in April. I logged on at 2 for what I thought would be twenty minutes, and it turned into a long back-and-forth with the vendor, who tried to sneak a price increase into the renewal. I asked for the old price, stopped typing, and waited. They agreed. Got it signed at 4:15, not 7:45, and no takeout at my desk, since my desk was my kitchen table. I sent Chloe a short note so she won't worry when she lands: renewal done, same price, enjoy the wedding. It felt good to be the backup instead of the owner. I used to want to own everything. Now I like that she owns this.
entries.favorite: Being the backup, not the owner
entries.highlight: Handled a vendor contract renewal on a holiday as Chloe's backup and kept the old price by negotiating.

entries.title: Forgot the buns for the roof
entries.body: Did the grocery run after coffee for the Fourth of July party on Alex's roof, which is now a tradition, the second year in a row. My job was burgers and a side. I got ground beef, cheese, tomatoes, red onions, lettuce, corn, a watermelon, and stuff for a potato salad. $91. Got home, made the potato salad, packed the cooler, and realized I forgot the buns. The buns. The one thing you need for burgers. I stood in my kitchen holding a watermelon, the same way I stood holding a clementine after the onion incident in December 2024. Except this time, I just texted Sam, who was on the way and stopped at a store. Problem solved in one text. Then on the roof, fireworks over the lake at 9:30. Robin cried a little, saying next year we'll be married. We all clinked plastic cups. Got home at midnight.
entries.highlight: Shopped for the Fourth of July rooftop party, forgot the buns, and enjoyed fireworks with friends for the second year.

entries.title: A standup that should've been an email
entries.body: Started with standup, which ran long, thirty-five minutes. Frankly, it could have been an email. The backend team announced that the 4.0 code freeze is moving again, from August to early September, and then everybody had an opinion. Got nothing else done until 3. Ate lunch at my desk again, because of the pre-vacation crunch. I'm leaving for the beach tomorrow, and I wanted to tie up loose ends. But here's the difference from last year. Last year before vacation, I gave Marcus a long list and worried the whole first day. This year, I spent thirty minutes with Chloe and Tomas this afternoon, gave them the decisions that are theirs to make, and wrote down the two that aren't. Then I set my out of office and told them I trust them, out loud, which felt corny and was true. Leaving my laptop at the office.
entries.highlight: Sat through a long standup about another 4.0 delay, then handed off decisions to Chloe and Tomas before vacation.

entries.title: Back at the gray cottage
entries.body: First day of a week at the beach. We rented the same little gray cottage as last year, with the porch that sags and the outdoor shower that is still the best thing I've ever experienced. Sam, Alex, Robin, and this year Priya too, who took the whole week off for the first time since she started nursing. $340 each this time, since we split it five ways. I turned off work notifications before we even got on the highway, and I didn't feel the little jolt of panic like I did last year. That's the difference: last year, turning them off was an act of courage. This year, it's just what I do on vacation. I read a whole book, start to finish, a mystery again, lying on a towel. Priya fell asleep in the sun and got a sunburn in the shape of her book. Alex and Robin are planning the wedding on the porch. My shoulders already dropped.
entries.favorite: Notifications off, no jolt of panic
entries.highlight: Started a beach vacation at the same cottage as last year with friends, including Priya, and turned off notifications without anxiety.

entries.title: Eight-minute handoff with Chloe
entries.body: This morning at 7:30, before Sam picked us up, I had a quick call with Chloe. She asked for it, which I liked. She wanted to confirm one thing about the 4.0 settings screen, and she had already decided what she'd do, and she just wanted me to hear it. It was the right call. I told her that. Then she asked how I'd handle it if the backend team slipped again while I was gone, and I said, you'll handle it however you think is best, and you'll be fine, and if you're not, you'll learn something. She laughed and said, that's what you always say. I guess it is. The whole call took eight minutes. Last year, my pre-vacation handoff was an anxious list for Marcus. This year, it was eight minutes with someone who didn't need me. Then I turned my phone's work apps off, for real, and put the phone in my bag.
entries.highlight: Had a short pre-vacation handoff call with Chloe, who had already made her own decision and needed little guidance.

entries.title: Sunrise run, three miles this time
entries.body: Day three at the beach. I got up at 5:40 and ran on the beach at sunrise again, on the hard sand by the water, like last year. Last year, I made it a mile and a half, and my calves were screaming after ten minutes. This year, I ran three miles. Out to the jetty and back. My calves still complained, because sand is sand, but they were complaining at mile two instead of minute ten. The pelicans were there again, flying low in a line, or maybe different pelicans, I can't tell. I stood in the cold water afterward up to my knees, and the sun came up pink, and I thought about last year, standing in this exact spot, feeling like I'd escaped something. This year, I didn't feel like I was escaping anything. I just felt like I was here. Back at the cottage, Sam was making French toast. Some things are tradition now.
entries.highlight: Ran three miles on the beach at sunrise, double the distance from the same run a year earlier.

entries.title: A new sticky note from Ravi
entries.body: Did weights at the gym after work, back from the beach. I finally asked Ravi for a new plan, since the old sticky note from June 2025 has completely faded on my water bottle. He wrote a new one, this time on an index card, which felt fitting. Deadlifts with a kettlebell, split squats, overhead press, rows, planks, three sets of eight to ten. Heavier than the first plan. The opera curls guy was there, as always, with a new opera. Halfway through, I noticed I was lifting the weight I used to warm up with as a working weight. That's a year of showing up, adding up. The split squats are a form of punishment, and my glutes will be talking about them until the weekend. I taped the new card onto the water bottle over the old faded sticky note. I didn't take the old one off. I like seeing them both.
entries.favorite: Keeping the old sticky note under the new card
entries.highlight: Started a heavier strength plan from Ravi and noticed their warm-up weight from last year is now a working weight.

entries.title: Retro on the beta, run by Chloe
entries.body: The 8:05 showed up fifteen minutes late. Cleared my inbox on the platform, which only took five minutes, because nobody needed me while I was away, which is the best possible review of my vacation handoff. Got in just in time for the retro on the 4.0 beta. Chloe ran it, the second time she's run a retro, and this one was much bigger, the whole release team, twenty people. She started by asking everyone what surprised them, which was a great question that I'd never thought of. A backend engineer said the beta users liked the new navigation more than he expected, which is a big deal, since that's Tomas's work. I didn't say much in the retro. Dana sat next to me and wrote something on her notepad and slid it to me. It said, this is what I meant. I knew she meant the ownership feedback from two years ago. I folded the paper and kept it.
entries.favorite: Dana's note: this is what I meant
entries.highlight: Watched Chloe run a large 4.0 beta retro, and Dana passed Jordan a note recognizing their growth in building ownership in others.

entries.title: Saturday spin, Omar's birthday ride
entries.body: Saturday morning spin with Omar. It was his birthday, so the whole playlist was songs from the year he was born, which turned out to be 1991, which made me feel old. He wore a sparkly headband. The class sang him happy birthday at the top of a climb, which sounded terrible, because we were all out of breath. I left buzzing, and then I did my whole Saturday reset: groceries, laundry, the Friday reset that I'd skipped yesterday, and a long call with Sam, who had one more round in June and still hasn't heard back. It's been a month. Sam is trying not to check their email every hour and failing. I told Sam about Mom's garlic patience. Sam said, if you say garlic patience one more time, I'm leaving the group chat. It's been about twelve weeks of three workouts a week. I'm keeping count, quietly.
entries.highlight: Took a birthday-themed spin class, did weekend chores, and encouraged Sam, who is still waiting to hear about a job.

entries.title: Chili verde for a summer Sunday
entries.body: Spent the afternoon on something new, chili verde, a pork chili with tomatillos, poblanos, jalapenos, onions, garlic, cumin, and a big bunch of cilantro. It's my summer version of Mom's red chili, which I now make almost without thinking. I charred the tomatillos and peppers under the broiler until they blistered, then blended them into the sauce, and simmered it with the pork in the Dutch oven for two hours. Listened to a long podcast about a woman who restores old pianos, which was oddly moving. I tasted it before adding salt, of course. My salt lessons have stuck for almost three months now. It came out tangy and bright and very spicy, maybe a little too spicy for Priya, who I brought a bowl to. She ate the whole thing anyway, crying a little, and said she'd be fine. Will definitely make it again, with one less jalapeno. Froze four portions for the busy weeks ahead.
entries.favorite: Priya crying and eating it anyway
entries.highlight: Made a tomatillo chili verde from scratch and stocked the freezer for busy weeks ahead.

entries.title: Focus morning on beta feedback
entries.body: Guarded my morning for the 4.0 beta feedback, which takes real effort in the middle of a release. There were two hundred comments from the fifty beta customers, and I went through every one and sorted them into three piles: fix before launch, fix after launch, and things we'll never fix but are funny. My favorite in the last pile was a customer who said the new blue was too cheerful for a Monday. Got a full draft of the summary done before lunch. Then I did something I'm getting better at: I didn't send it to Dana right away. I sent it to Chloe and Tomas first, so they could add what I missed. Tomas added three things, and one was important. Then I sent it to Dana. A year ago, I would have wanted to be the one who knew everything first. Now, I want the summary to be right. That's a different goal.
entries.highlight: Sorted two hundred pieces of beta feedback during focus time and had teammates review the summary before sending it to Dana.

entries.title: Couch interviews, and Tomas leads one
entries.body: Worked from home today. Did laundry between calls. Got through interview feedback from the couch, for the new designer we're hiring to help with 4.0 and onboarding next year. This time I wasn't on the panel alone. Tomas led one of the interviews himself, his first one, and he asked the candidate about a design decision she was proudest of, and then about one she regretted, which is a great combination. His written feedback was better than mine was the first time I did this, back in December 2024, when I wrote feedback like a cooking show judge. I told him that, and he was quiet for a second and then said, I learned from your feedback on me. That's the thing about mentoring, I think. You don't see it working until someone else is doing it. Ate lunch at my desk, which is the couch. But it was outside on the window ledge, partly.
entries.favorite: Tomas saying he learned from my feedback
entries.highlight: Wrote interview feedback from home and saw Tomas lead his first interview using lessons learned from Jordan.

entries.title: Thirteen weeks, and a rest day on purpose
entries.body: Skipped the workout and went to bed at 9:30. Needed it. But I'm marking today as something, because I did the math this morning: thirteen weeks in a row of three workouts a week, since the race in April. That's the longest streak of my life. Longer than the running plan, longer than the fall swims. And it's not because I'm chasing anything. There's no race, no finish line, no index card goal. I just do it now, the way I brush my teeth. Today I was tired from the beta work and the heat, and I took a rest day on purpose, and I didn't feel even a little bit guilty, because I know I'll be back on Saturday. That's the part that's new. In the winter, one missed workout was the first domino. Now it's just a Thursday. My body was telling me to slow down, and I listened, because I trust myself to start again.
entries.highlight: Reached a thirteen-week streak of three workouts a week and took a guilt-free rest day, trusting the habit to hold.

entries.title: Priya's day-shift news at the Ethiopian place
entries.body: Met Priya for dinner at the Ethiopian place around the corner, our place now. The owner brought out the vegetarian combination before we even ordered, which is the highest honor I can imagine. Priya had news: she's been offered a day-shift job as a charge nurse on her unit, starting in October. After six years of nights. She was nervous to take it, because she likes her night team, but she said she wants to see daylight on purpose, not just on the way home. I told her about the apartment that made me see daylight on purpose. She said, that's different, and I said, is it? We talked for a long time about change, and how the scary part is usually before, not during. Then we laughed so hard about Gerald's wedding gig, which apparently ended with him playing a solo during the cake cutting that nobody asked for, that the owner brought us free tea again. Stayed until they closed.
entries.highlight: Had dinner with Priya, who was offered a day-shift charge nurse job after six years of nights.

entries.title: Back-to-back until the code freeze
entries.body: Started with standup, which ran long, twenty-eight minutes, because the 4.0 code freeze is in four weeks and everyone is anxious. Then back-to-back calls until lunch. Got nothing else done until 3. This is the crunch part of a big release, and I recognize it from last year's empty states launch, but bigger. Here's what I'm trying to do differently: I'm protecting two things no matter what. Lunch away from my desk, even if it's just fifteen minutes on the bench, and leaving by 6. Today, I got the lunch, a quick one, leftover chili verde from the freezer in a thermos. I did not get the leaving by 6. I left at 6:40. That's not terrible. Chloe and Tomas left at 5:30, because I told them to, and this time it wasn't the sneaky do-it-myself version. Their work was done. Mine wasn't, because I'm still in too many meetings. That's the next thing to fix.
entries.favorite: Lunch on the bench, even fifteen minutes
entries.highlight: Faced a meeting-heavy day before the 4.0 code freeze while trying to protect lunch breaks and reasonable hours.

entries.title: Heat wave, early bed again
entries.body: No workout tonight. I'll be asleep before 10, and I need it. It's the second rest day in a week, and that would have worried me last winter, but today I know why. It was 96 degrees, the train's air conditioning was broken, and I got home at 7:20 looking like I'd been swimming in my clothes. Some days the weather wins. I took a cold shower, ate a cucumber salad standing in front of the fan, and called it a day. I'm still at three workouts a week, technically, since I did a long swim on Sunday and weights yesterday morning. The streak is fine. I used to treat streaks like a glass that would shatter if I dropped it once. I'm treating it more like a rope now. It can stretch and still hold. I'll swim on Thursday, at 6:15am, before the heat. The fan is pointed right at my face.
entries.favorite: Streak as a rope, not glass
entries.highlight: Rested during a heat wave and noted their workout habit now feels flexible rather than fragile.

entries.title: Lentil and sausage stew, salt relapse
entries.body: First attempt at a lentil and sausage stew today, with French green lentils, smoked sausage, carrots, celery, onion, garlic, thyme, and a splash of red wine vinegar at the end. It's a fall recipe, really, but the heat wave broke this morning and it was 71 and rainy, so it felt right. The problem was the sausage. Smoked sausage is basically salt in a casing, and I salted the broth like I would for regular lentil soup. I tasted it. I always taste now. But I tasted before the sausage had released its salt, so it seemed fine, and then an hour later it was way too much. My first salt relapse since April. I'll adjust next time: no salt until the end, the sausage does the work. Listened to a podcast about the people who design highway signs, which was oddly relevant to my job. Froze three portions anyway. Salty soup is still soup.
entries.highlight: Made a lentil and sausage stew that ended up salty from the sausage, their first salt slip in months.

entries.title: Short list for a crunch week
entries.body: Went to the grocery store at 8, and made the list short and strategic, because the next four weeks before the code freeze are going to be busy, and I want easy food. Spinach, yogurt, chicken thighs, rice, eggs, a big bag of frozen dumplings for emergencies, frozen peas, tortillas, cheese, and peaches, because it's August and the peaches are perfect. $77. Stuck to the list. I've been doing this for so long now that I don't really think about it. I just check the pantry and the freezer list on the door, then I write the list, then I buy the list. When I started doing this in January 2025, it felt like a big, disciplined thing. Now it's like brushing my teeth. I ate a peach in the parking lot, standing over the trunk of my car so the juice wouldn't get on my shirt. It got on my shirt anyway.
entries.highlight: Did a short, strategic grocery run to prepare easy food for the busy weeks before the 4.0 code freeze.

entries.title: Long walk at dawn with Dad on the phone
entries.body: Did a long walk before work, on the lake path at 6, before the heat. Halfway to the lighthouse, my phone rang, and it was Dad, which still surprises me every time. He was on his own morning walk, his mile a day, which Deshawn assigned him when PT ended. So we walked together, on the phone, a train ride apart. He described his route, which is past the library, then the church with the ugly new sign, and back. I described mine, the lake and the lighthouse and the guy with the metal detector. He asked how fast I walk and I said I don't know, and he said, I do about twenty-two minutes for my mile. He sounded proud, which made me proud. When we hung up, I'd walked farther than I planned. I got to my desk with the whole call still in my head, like a song. I want to do this every Wednesday. I'm going to ask him tonight.
entries.favorite: Walking together a train ride apart
entries.highlight: Took a dawn walk by the lake while Dad called during his own daily walk, and they walked together over the phone.

entries.title: Friday weights, heavier kettlebell
entries.body: Did weights at the gym before work, Ravi's index card plan. I moved up to the next kettlebell for the deadlifts this morning, which was a big moment for me and nobody else. The opera curls guy didn't even look up. I felt slow on the overhead press, which I'm still bad at, but I showed up. It's interesting how my reasons for exercising have changed. In January 2025 it was a goal on a card. In the spring, it was the race. Now, frankly, it's mostly this: I'm a nicer person on the days I move. I'm more patient in meetings, I'm calmer at the Friday standup, and I don't snap at the late train. I didn't know that was the real benefit. Nobody puts that on a poster at the gym. I took a photo of the new kettlebell, which is a very strange thing to take a photo of, and sent it to Ravi.
entries.highlight: Lifted a heavier kettlebell at the gym and reflected that exercise now mostly helps them stay patient and calm.

entries.title: Mom and Dad stayed over
entries.body: Mom and Dad came for the weekend and stayed over at my apartment, the first time they've ever stayed at my place. In the old apartment, it would have been impossible. There was nowhere to put them. This time I bought a good sofa bed mattress topper, set up the living room for them, and slept in my own bed while they slept in the room with the good light. Dad climbed the stairs without the railing. He made a point of it. Mom brought a bag of tomatoes and a tray of zinnias for my windowsill. We walked the lake path together in the evening, the three of us, the full mile, at Dad's pace, which is faster than it used to be. Then I made them dinner with the Dutch oven, chicken and white beans and Mom's tomatoes. Dad said, this kid can cook now. Mom said, I know, I taught them. This morning, Mom made coffee in my kitchen like she lives here. I loved it.
entries.favorite: Dad saying this kid can cook now
entries.highlight: Hosted their parents for an overnight stay for the first time, with Dad walking the lake path and climbing stairs without a railing.

entries.title: Mom's chili, from memory now
entries.body: Made Mom's red chili for dinner tonight, with some of her tomatoes from the weekend instead of canned. I don't use the recipe card anymore. The first time I made this, in February 2025, I followed it like a science experiment and texted her a photo, and she said it needed more cumin. Now I add more cumin automatically, plus her pinch of love, which I still think is brown sugar, plus a little smoked paprika, which is my addition. It's my version now. Listened to a podcast about the history of chili, which apparently caused fights in Texas for a hundred years. Two lunches and two freezer portions came out of the pot. I'm getting ready for code freeze week. I sent Mom a photo, out of habit, and she replied, you added something. How does she know that from a photo? She's never been wrong about my chili.
entries.highlight: Made Mom's chili from memory with their own additions, and Mom spotted the change from a photo.

entries.title: The lobby free table
entries.body: Our building has a free table in the lobby, where people leave things they don't need, and I've been quietly taking from it for a year: a lamp, a set of mugs, a stack of mystery novels. Tonight I gave back. After work, I cleaned out my kitchen cabinets and put out a bread machine I've used once, a second colander, the old dull knife from before the chef's knife, six mismatched glasses, and a crepe maker I got as a gift and never opened. Within an hour, everything was gone except the knife, which frankly tracks. Gerald took the crepe maker and said he'll make crepes for the building on Sunday. I don't know if that's a threat or a promise. The cabinets look huge now. I put the knife in the donation bag for the weekend. I like being part of a building where things go around, instead of out.
entries.highlight: Put unused kitchen items on the building's free table, and neighbor Gerald took the crepe maker.

entries.title: Friday prep for code freeze week
entries.body: Meal-prepped lunches for next week tonight, since code freeze is coming and I know myself. Chili, the batch from Wednesday plus the freezer stash, with rice and roasted broccoli in five containers. It took about an hour, including the dishes. Tuesday has nine meetings on it, so Tuesday's lunch needed to already exist. I've gotten fast at this. In November 2024 my first meal prep took two hours and made four watery soups. Tonight it was an hour and made five good lunches, plus I cleaned the kitchen while things roasted, which is a skill nobody tells you about. Mom calls it cleaning as you go. I call it not wanting to do it later. I also restocked the freezer list on the door: two chili verde, three lentil stew, one red lentil coconut, two dumplings. That's my safety net for the crunch. Different kind of emergency fund, but the same idea.
entries.highlight: Meal-prepped a week of chili lunches in an hour before the code freeze and restocked the freezer.

entries.title: Saturday stir-fry with Gerald's crepes
entries.body: Gerald did in fact make crepes for the building this morning, in the lobby, with the crepe maker from the free table, and they were good. He played one song on the trumpet between batches. Then tonight I made a stir-fry for dinner, my standard rotation one, but with what was left from the farmers market: green beans, a zucchini, some corn, and the tofu, pressed and crisped. No podcast needed, because Gerald was practicing scales on the third floor the whole time. The sauce is the same as always, but I've added a spoon of peanut butter, which I learned from Priya, and it's very good. Code freeze is Monday. I feel ready, which is a strange feeling before a big work week. The food is prepped, the freezer is full, and the team knows the plan. I'm not even nervous. Just a little tired, and very full of crepes.
entries.highlight: Enjoyed neighbor Gerald's lobby crepe breakfast and made a stir-fry, feeling prepared for the code freeze.

entries.title: Code freeze swim
entries.body: Code freeze was yesterday, and it went fine. Tonight I swam after work, partly to celebrate and partly because my shoulders were tied in knots from two days of hunching over specs. The pool was almost empty. Bev was there, in a new swim cap, blue with yellow flowers. I did forty laps tonight, the most ever, and ten in a row without stopping. I felt strong today. When I got out, Bev said, you swim like you've been doing this for years now. I told her it's been a year, exactly, since my first swim here, right after I moved. She said, that's years in pool time. I don't know what that means, but I liked it. I got home and ate leftover stir-fry on the couch in my bathrobe, and fell asleep at 9:45 with the window open. One of those small perfect evenings that's easy to forget, so I'm writing it down.
entries.favorite: Bev saying years in pool time
entries.highlight: Swam a personal best of forty laps after the 4.0 code freeze, a year after first swimming at the new gym.

entries.title: Spin on my moving anniversary
entries.body: Did spin after work with Omar, who announced that tonight's playlist was all songs about moving on, which was a coincidence, because today is the one year anniversary of moving into this apartment. My legs had plenty left, and I sang along to most of the songs under my breath. Afterward I bought a small cake from the bakery by the lake and took it across the hall, and Priya and I ate it on my floor, in the square of evening light, like the pizza on moving day. She asked what changed most this year, and I thought about it. I said I used to wait for things, for someone to notice me at work, for the right time to ask, for motivation to exercise. And now I mostly don't wait. I just start. She said, that's a good year. It was a good year.
entries.favorite: Cake on the floor in the light
entries.highlight: Celebrated the one-year anniversary of moving with spin class and cake with Priya, reflecting on no longer waiting to start things.

entries.title: New rent, updated autopay
entries.body: Checked the bills this morning. The new rent kicked in this month, $1,915, the two-year rate I asked for in June. I updated the rent autopay, which I almost forgot, which would have been a very funny way to mess up a whole year of good money habits. Also set up autopay for the new renter's insurance amount, which went up two dollars. Also canceled the meditation app I signed up for in the winter slump and opened three times. I think I meditate more on the lake path than I ever did with the app. That's $70 a year. I looked back at the first bills entry I did in this apartment, a year ago. I wrote that I was paying for light. I still am, and I still think it's worth it. But I've also stopped paying for a lot of things I don't use, so the light is cheaper than it looked.
entries.highlight: Updated autopay for the new negotiated rent and canceled an unused meditation app subscription.

entries.title: Labor Day budget and a near goal
entries.body: Labor Day, a day off, so I did the monthly budget check-in for August on the window ledge with coffee. Eating out was $198, a little high because of the code freeze. Every night out had a reason, but some of those reasons were just I'm tired, which doesn't count under my rule. Groceries were a normal $224. The real news is the emergency fund. It's at $9,640. The goal I wrote on the index card in January was three months of expenses, which I calculated as $10,000. I'm $360 away. Last year on Labor Day I was in Tamsin's spin class, then packing the last boxes, then eating dumplings on the floor of the old apartment, with about $600 left after the move. I'm going to hit the goal next month, two months early. I'm trying not to think about what to do with the extra. Probably the brakes, eventually. Cars always need something.
entries.highlight: Reviewed the August budget on Labor Day and found the emergency fund just $360 short of the three-month goal.

entries.title: Alex on Sam's new job
entries.body: Got coffee with Alex this morning near the park, and we walked around the block twice, like old times. Sam couldn't come because Sam starts the new job on Monday, at the climate organization, the communications job, after almost a year of looking, and is spending the weekend, quote, being nervous efficiently. Alex and I talked about it the whole time. How Sam never gave up, two rejections, all those cover letters. Alex said, Sam did the garlic thing, and I laughed, because I've apparently told everyone about Mom's garlic. Then wedding talk: Alex and Robin picked the lodge menu and the colors, green and gold, and Alex asked if I'd give a reading at the ceremony. I said yes, of course, and then immediately panicked about public speaking, and then remembered I've done an all-hands and a client call. I can read a poem. Alex says the three of us need a dinner soon. We do.
entries.highlight: Had coffee with Alex about Sam's new climate job starting Monday and agreed to give a reading at Alex's wedding.

entries.title: Bulgogi stir-fry, soy times two
entries.body: Bulgogi-style beef stir-fry tonight, my first try, with thinly sliced beef marinated in soy sauce, pear, garlic, ginger, sesame oil, and a little sugar, then seared fast in the cast iron with onions and scallions. The problem was I marinated the beef and then also added soy sauce to the pan, because that's how my regular stir-fry sauce works. Double soy. Too much salt. Again. I'm starting to think my salt mistakes are just a personality trait now. I'll adjust next time: the marinade is the sauce, no extra soy. I read about people who climb mountains without oxygen while it marinated, which put my salt problem in perspective. Ate it over a lot of plain rice, which helps, and with cucumber kimchi Priya brought over. I texted Sam a photo for good luck tomorrow, the first day of the new job. Sam replied with a picture of an ironed shirt.
entries.highlight: Tried a bulgogi-style beef stir-fry that came out salty from doubled soy sauce and sent Sam good luck for the new job.

entries.title: Harissa chicken at 9pm
entries.body: Late dinner tonight, and a new one: harissa sheet-pan chicken, with chicken thighs, chickpeas, red onion, lemon, and harissa paste. But I didn't start cooking until 8:15, because the 4.0 launch got moved again, to October, after a backend bug, and the whole design team spent the afternoon re-planning. Dinner at 9pm. The recipe said a teaspoon of salt, plus the harissa, and harissa has salt in it too. I put in the teaspoon anyway, because I was tired and following directions. Too much salt. Will adjust next time: half the salt when the paste is already salty. Worth a rematch, because it was smoky and spicy and the chickpeas got crispy. I didn't go to the gym today or yesterday, and probably won't tomorrow. I can feel the crunch coming. I'm going to try to keep the walks, at least. And the freezer is full, which is the best thing I did this month.
entries.highlight: Made a harissa sheet-pan chicken late after the 4.0 launch was pushed again, and felt the work crunch cutting into gym time.

entries.title: Crunch week walk to the lighthouse
entries.body: Did a long walk after work on Saturday, which is technically after working from home for four hours on a Saturday, which is the crunch. The launch is now October 15th. I walked to the lighthouse and back, about two miles, and felt good the whole way, even though I haven't been to the gym all week. I walked fast, the way you walk when you're trying to shake a spreadsheet out of your head. The lake was rough and gray and the wind was cold, the first cold wind of the fall. I know what this time of year does to me. Last October I wrote about the dark coming back. This year I'm trying to be smarter about it. I've already put the light lamp back on my desk, and I've booked swims for after the launch, even if I can't go before. The gym will wait. I'll be back. I know that now in a way I didn't last year.
entries.favorite: The first cold wind of fall
entries.highlight: Took a long walk during a work crunch week and prepared for the darker season, confident they will return to the gym.

entries.title: Mom's fall harvest call
entries.body: Called Mom on the walk home from the grocery store. She's in the fall harvest, the last tomatoes, a lot of squash, and the zinnias are taller than she is. The heirloom seeds I mailed her in May turned into a purple tomato she says is the best she's ever grown. Dad says hi. He's walking a mile and a half a day now, past the library and the church with the ugly sign, and then an extra loop by the school. He wants to do a charity walk in the spring, a 5K, and he said, if you can run one, I can walk one. I told him I'll walk it with him. We talked until the ice cream in my bag went soft. Mom asked if I was working too much, because she can always hear it in my voice. I said yes, until October 15th. She said, and then? I said, and then I'm going to ask for the next big thing. I made plans to call again next Sunday.
entries.highlight: Had a long call with Mom about the fall harvest and learned Dad wants to walk a charity 5K in the spring.

entries.title: Twenty-minute reset in a messy week
entries.body: Crunch week, and the apartment shows it. Dishes in the sink, laundry on the chair, mail piled on the counter, and three days of coffee cups by my desk. On Sunday afternoon I set a timer for twenty minutes and did the fastest possible version of my Friday reset. Dishes, one load of laundry, mail sorted, coffee cups washed, recycling out. I didn't do the sheets or the fix-it thing. Twenty minutes, and the apartment went from overwhelming to fine. I used to think that if I couldn't do something all the way, there was no point. Like with the gym, or the budget, or cleaning. Now I think the twenty-minute version is what keeps things from falling apart in busy weeks. It doesn't have to be perfect. It has to be enough. I also wrote a list for the next two weeks, and the last item on it, in capital letters, is ask Dana.
entries.highlight: Did a quick twenty-minute apartment reset during a crunch week and wrote a reminder to ask Dana about leading onboarding.

entries.title: Emergency fund: three months, done
entries.body: Did the bills tonight, which means checking that the autopay ran, which it did, rent, electric, gas, internet, insurance. Canceled a subscription I never use, the last one I could find, a magazine I got as a gift that auto-renewed. And then I looked at the emergency fund, and it's at $10,080. Three months of expenses. The goal from the index card on New Year's Day, done two months early. I sat on the couch with my laptop for a while just looking at it. Two years ago, in November 2024, I had zero in savings and $412 of takeout in one month, and I made a four column spreadsheet because I didn't know what else to do. Now I have three months of not having to panic. If the car breaks, if I get sick, if something happens to Mom and Dad, I can handle it. That's what this money is, really. Not money. Calm. I'm going to keep the automatic transfer going, but slower.
entries.highlight: Reached the goal of a three-month emergency fund two months early, two years after starting with no savings.

entries.title: Market salmon for Priya and Gerald
entries.body: After the market and coffee, I went back for a second round, because Priya and I decided to do a building dinner tonight. I bought fresh pasta, a piece of salmon from the seafood counter, and a second loaf of sourdough. Priya invited Gerald. So I made the miso glazed salmon I first tried last December, the sticky one, plus the fresh pasta with brown butter and sage from Priya's balcony, and an apple crumble with the market apples. I measured the salt. I tasted. It was right. Gerald brought a bottle of wine and did not bring his trumpet, which Priya had specifically requested. We ate at my little table with Priya's two extra chairs, the same ones she brought over for my first dinner party last December. Gerald told stories about playing in a band in the 70s, which were mostly about vans breaking down. I'm so glad I live here.
entries.highlight: Hosted a building dinner for Priya and Gerald with miso salmon, fresh pasta, and apple crumble from market ingredients.

entries.title: Clocks back, winter plan on the fridge
entries.body: The clocks went back last night, and it got dark at 4:58 today. Last year this is when the slump started, quietly, a skipped swim here and a takeout night there, until I was barely leaving the couch by January. So this afternoon I made a winter plan, and put it on the fridge, on an index card, of course. One: the light lamp on the desk, every morning, twenty minutes. Two: swims booked on Wednesdays and Saturdays through February, already in the app. Three: freezer nights on Tuesdays and Thursdays, freezer stocked. Four: one plan with a person every week, Priya, Sam, Alex, a call with Dad on his walk. Five: when I skip something, I don't skip the next one. Then I crossed three things off the list: swapped the sheets to flannel, put the winter coat by the door, and changed the batteries in the smoke detector. Ready, or as ready as I can be.
entries.highlight: Made a written winter plan with light, swimming, freezer meals, and social plans to avoid last year's seasonal slump.

entries.title: Recovery chili in the Dutch oven
entries.body: Feeling about seventy percent better today, so I worked from home a half day and then made chili for dinner, because the freezer list on the door was looking thin after the sick day. Mom's red chili, my version, with the extra cumin and smoked paprika, in the big red Dutch oven my parents gave me last Christmas. Listened to a podcast about the history of chicken soup while making chili, which felt like cheating on soup. It turned out better than expected, but frankly, it always does now. Enough leftovers for two days, plus four portions for the freezer, written on the list. Two years ago I couldn't make this because I forgot the onions. Last year I made it from the recipe card. Now I make it from memory, sick, on a Friday, without thinking. I think that's what it means to really learn something. You stop noticing that you know it.
entries.highlight: Made Mom's chili from memory while recovering from a cold and restocked the freezer.

entries.title: Saturday run, slow and grateful
entries.body: Did a 30-minute run this morning before I could talk myself out of it, the first run since the sore throat. Slow, but my legs remembered. I ran the river loop near my old neighborhood, for the first time in over a year, just to see it. Past the bakery that smelled like bread at 6am, past the duck man's bench, empty today, past the station where I used to catch the 8:05. I thought about that version of me, eating lunch at my desk, wincing at the takeout number, clapping for my own work with someone else's name on it, waiting for someone to notice. I wanted to tell that person something, but I don't know what I'd say. Maybe just: it gets lighter. Then I took the train home, sat by the window, and watched the lake come into view. Later, a long nap with the sun on the hallway rug. Thanksgiving in twelve days.
entries.highlight: Went for a 30-minute run past their old neighborhood after being sick and reflected on how much has changed in two years.

entries.title: Long call with Mom
entries.body: Called Mom while folding laundry on Sunday afternoon. Three loads, because the crunch left me with a mountain. She is planning the garden for spring already, even though she's still pulling out the summer plants, and she wants help building a raised bed, the one we were supposed to build in May before the lumber never came. She's already measured the spot and ordered the lumber early this time, to be delivered in March. I'm on the calendar for April. Dad's knee is better. Not perfect, she says it still knows when it's going to rain, but he walked to the farmers market and back yesterday, two miles, and carried the bag home. I told her about the 1:1 and asking Dana directly, and she said, I always knew you would, which isn't true, but it was nice to hear. We talked for an hour and a half. I folded everything, even the fitted sheet, badly.
entries.highlight: Had a long call with Mom about spring garden plans and building a raised bed, and heard Dad's knee is better.

entries.title: Oil change and tire rotation
entries.body: Dropped the car off before work for an oil change and tire rotation, and took the bus in, which was slower than the train but had a nice view of the lake. Mechanic said the brakes have maybe six months left. Two years ago, that sentence would have made my stomach drop. Today I just asked how much, and he said probably $450 to $550 for the front and back. I added it to the budget sheet, in a new line called brakes, with a target date of March. That's about $90 a month, which I can do without touching the emergency fund, which is for real emergencies, not things I know are coming. $96 total for today. I picked it up after work and drove it home the long way, by the lake, since I barely drive it and wanted to enjoy it. A known problem with a plan isn't really a problem. It's just a line in a spreadsheet.
entries.highlight: Got an oil change and tire rotation for $96, learned the brakes need replacing within six months, and added it to the budget calmly.

entries.title: Train was late again
entries.body: Left at 7:40 for the 8:05 train, which showed up at 8:25. Twenty minutes late. It was 44 degrees and the platform was full of people in their first fall jackets, all staring down the track like it owed them money. I used the wait to clear my inbox, which was mostly launch threads, and got it down to six. Standup ran long because the release got pushed, again, to the 15th, and the backend team needed to walk us through why, which took a while. It's fine. It's the right call. Better to ship it two weeks late than to ship it broken. Ate lunch at my desk, which I keep promising to stop doing. I did so well in the spring, three outdoor lunches a week. The crunch took that, and I let it. Two more weeks. Then I want my bench back, and the pigeons, and my lunch break.
entries.favorite: Clearing my inbox on the platform
entries.highlight: Waited for a late train, cleared their inbox on the platform, and sat through a long standup about the release being pushed.

entries.title: Big warehouse store trip
entries.body: Drove the car, brakes and all, to the big warehouse store for a stock-up trip, which I do every couple of months now that I have a pantry and a closet big enough for it. Stocked up: paper towels, olive oil, frozen berries, coffee beans, laundry detergent, and a giant bag of rice. Also impulse-bought a rug for the hallway, a blue and cream striped one that was just sitting there at the end of an aisle, looking at me. $212. Should last a month for everything but the rug. The rug will hopefully last years. I put it in the hallway as soon as I got home and it's perfect. The hallway, which I swept on my very first weekend here, now feels finished. I'm not going to beat myself up about the rug. It's in the budget sheet under home, and I can name exactly what I'm celebrating: two years of being a person who has a hallway worth a rug.
entries.highlight: Did a $212 warehouse store stock-up and impulse-bought a hallway rug, which they decided was worth it.

entries.title: Dentist appointment
entries.body: Cleaning at 4:30, and I took the afternoon off to make it, which I would never have done two years ago. I would have rushed from a meeting and been late and stressed. This time I just blocked the afternoon and nobody minded, because Chloe and Tomas had the launch prep covered. No cavities. Hygienist said to floss more, as always. She says it every time, and every time I promise, and then I floss for about nine days. I told her that straight, and she laughed and said nine days is above average. So I'm going to aim for ten. Picked up the dry cleaning on the way back, since it was next door, my one nice suit jacket, which I need for the launch party next week and the wedding next spring. Then I walked home along the lake in the late sun, at 5:30, on a Friday, with clean teeth. Not bad.
entries.highlight: Took the afternoon off for a dentist cleaning with no cavities, then picked up dry cleaning next door.

entries.title: Farmers market
entries.body: Walked to the farmers market Saturday morning, on the first truly crisp fall day, with the trees on my street almost fully orange. Bought apples, a loaf of sourdough from the bread woman, honey from the honey guy, who now gives me a sample without asking, and a small pumpkin for the porch, which is really the front steps of the building, but I'm calling it a porch. Last Halloween I didn't have a pumpkin at all. Ran into my neighbor Priya by the apple stand, and we got coffee after and sat on a bench in the park. She's been on day shift for two weeks and says she keeps being surprised by the sun, which I understand completely. We talked about the launch, and her new job, and how the both of us spent this whole year changing our schedules and getting more light. She said we should start a club. I said we already did. It's called the building.
entries.highlight: Bought apples, bread, honey, and a pumpkin at the farmers market and had coffee with neighbor Priya.

entries.title: Dinner with college friends
entries.body: Met Sam and Alex at the Thai place downtown, the one where we celebrated Alex's promotion back in May 2025. First time all three of us were in the same room since summer, because Sam's new job and Alex's wedding planning and my launch ate the whole fall. Talked about Sam's new job, which Sam loves, six weeks in. Sam writes about solar farms now and says it's the first job where they don't dread Sunday nights. Talked about Alex's wedding plans, which now include a seating chart that Alex described as a war crime, and a menu tasting at the lodge. I told them about asking Dana directly, and they both put down their chopsticks and clapped, which embarrassed me, in a good way. We laughed about the fire alarm, the frying pan, the pivot couch, all the old stories. Got home at 11, worth it.
entries.highlight: Had dinner with college friends Sam and Alex for the first time since summer, catching up on Sam's new job and Alex's wedding.

entries.title: Saturday grocery run
entries.body: Went to the store at 9 before it got busy. Got eggs, spinach, chicken thighs, rice, oat milk, bananas, and coffee. Forgot the dish soap, which was the main reason I went. The main reason. I had it in my head the whole way there, and then I saw the fall display of pumpkins by the door and it just fell out of my brain. Spent $84. I stood in my kitchen afterward with a carton of oat milk and remembered the onions in December 2024, and the buns on the Fourth, and laughed. Some things don't change, I guess. The difference is I don't spiral about it anymore. I just walked to the corner store and got dish soap for $3.49, which brings the real total to $87.49. Then I wrote dish soap on the list for next week too, just in case, because I don't trust myself near pumpkins.
entries.highlight: Did the Saturday grocery run early for $84 but forgot the dish soap, which was the main reason for going.

entries.title: Back to the gym
entries.body: First gym session in three weeks. The launch crunch took the gym, like I knew it would, but yesterday's 1:1 gave me so much energy that I went this morning at 6:30 before the train. Kept it light: 20 minutes on the bike, some rows and squats from Ravi's index card, at a lighter weight than in August. I didn't try to make up for three weeks in one morning. That's something I've learned. Legs were shaky on the stairs home, because I went home to shower first, but I feel more awake than I have all week. The opera curls guy was there and he nodded at me, which he has never done, so maybe he noticed I was gone. Last fall, three weeks off would have turned into three months. This time, it was three weeks, and then I came back, because I knew I would. The habit was still there, waiting for me.
entries.highlight: Returned to the gym after a three-week work-crunch break with a light session and felt more awake all week.

entries.title: Handing out candy
entries.body: Last Halloween, I bought one bag of candy and ran out by 6:45, and a tiny dragon was very disappointed in me. This year I learned. Bought two bags of candy on the way home and sat on the front steps with Priya, next to my farmers market pumpkin. Ran out by 7:30 anyway. I think the kids remembered our building. Best costume was a kid dressed as an astronaut with a cardboard jetpack made of two soda bottles painted silver, with tissue paper flames. He told me very seriously that he was going to Mars after he finished his candy. Priya gave him two pieces. Gerald came down dressed as a pirate and played a sea shanty on the trumpet, which the kids loved and the parents tolerated. Then I went inside and carved the farmers market pumpkin, a simple face, while listening to a scary podcast. Next year: three bags.
entries.highlight: Handed out two bags of candy on the front steps with Priya, ran out by 7:30, and carved the farmers market pumpkin.

entries.title: Release finally shipped
entries.body: The release went out at 2pm. 4.0, after two delays and seven months of work. I was in a room with Elena, Marcus, Ravi, Chloe, and Tomas, and Marcus pressed the button, and then we all just stared at the dashboards for twenty minutes, waiting for something to break. A couple of small bugs came in, a misaligned icon and a button that said undefined in one language, but nothing major. Chloe and Tomas fixed both before 3. The team ordered tacos to celebrate, a huge spread from the taco truck by the office, and Dana gave a short speech and said my name and Chloe's and Tomas's, all three, which is exactly how I wanted it. I left at 5 on the dot for the first time in two weeks. On the train home, I thought about the onboarding spec I wrote in January 2025, alone, until 7:45. This time, I didn't do it alone. That was the best part.
entries.highlight: The 4.0 release shipped smoothly after months of work, the team celebrated with tacos, and Jordan left on time for the first time in weeks.

entries.title: Meal prep Sunday
entries.body: Cooked a big pot of rice, roasted chicken and broccoli, and portioned out five lunches. Took about two hours with a podcast on, a long one about the history of the subway map. The chicken got a crust in the cast iron before going in the oven, which is my trick now. Kitchen looks like a disaster, with a rice pot, two sheet pans, the cast iron, and broccoli bits on every surface, but weekday me will be grateful. Especially Tuesday me, who has a 1:1 with Dana and something important to ask. I put the five containers in a row in the fridge, like soldiers, the same way I did my first good meal prep in the new kitchen last October, and sent Mom a photo, because I always do. She replied, you've done this before. Yes, Mom. A lot of times now. Then I cleaned the kitchen. It took longer than the cooking.
entries.highlight: Spent two hours on Sunday meal prep, making five lunches of rice, chicken, and broccoli for a big week.

entries.title: 1:1 with my manager
entries.body: Talked through the roadmap with Dana in our 1:1 this afternoon, mostly the launch on the 15th and the Q4 plan after it. And then I brought up wanting to lead the onboarding redesign. Not a hint. Not I'm definitely interested. I said, I want to lead onboarding, here's why, and I sent her the two page document I wrote in February, the one that's been sitting in my drafts for eight months, updated with everything from 4.0. Then I stopped talking. That was the hardest part, the silence. Dana read the first page while I sat there. Then she said yes, pending the Q4 plan, which gets finalized next week, but she said she'd already been planning to put my name in, and she was glad I asked first. Felt good to ask for it directly instead of hinting. Two years of hints, and one sentence did it. I walked to the train feeling about ten feet tall.
entries.highlight: Directly asked Dana to lead the onboarding redesign, and Dana said yes pending the Q4 plan.

entries.title: Quarterly review
entries.body: Had my quarterly review with Dana. Feedback was mostly positive: the workshop and the release were called out by name, and she said three other directors mentioned the workshop to her, which I didn't know. She also mentioned Chloe and Tomas, and how they've grown, and said that's part of my work too, now. Growth area is delegating more instead of doing everything myself. Fair. Completely fair. I thought about the Friday in May when I sent the team home and wrote the spec alone, and the crunch in September when I took back pieces I'd handed off. I'm better at it than I was. But when I'm stressed, I still grab everything. Dana said the onboarding redesign is too big for anyone to do alone, so this is the year I have to really learn it. I wrote one word in my notebook after the meeting: let. Let them do it. Let it be different from how I'd do it.
entries.highlight: Had a mostly positive quarterly review praising the workshop and release, with delegating more as the main growth area.

entries.title: First 5K in a while
entries.body: Ran a full 5K without stopping for the first time since spring. Since the race in April, the one with the man dressed as a banana. I did it on the lake path after work, out past the lighthouse and back, in the cold, under the lamps, with the lighthouse blinking green every four seconds like it always does. 31 minutes, slow but steady. That's three minutes faster than the race, and I wasn't even trying to be fast. I was just trying to keep going. The gym visits are adding up. The swims with Bev, the weights from Ravi's card, Omar's spin, Hal's yoga. None of it was about running, but all of it was. When I got home I called Dad, who was on his evening walk, and told him. He said, 31? and I said, 31. He said, I'm doing my mile in nineteen now. We're both getting faster. Then I stretched on the hallway rug.
entries.highlight: Ran a full 5K without stopping in 31 minutes, three minutes faster than the spring race, thanks to consistent gym work.

entries.title: Sick day
entries.body: Woke up with a sore throat and called out. Two years ago, I would have worked anyway, from bed, answering every message, and felt worse for three extra days. Today I sent one message to Dana and the team at 7:30, then put my laptop in the closet. Soup, tea, and two naps. The soup was the lentil soup from the freezer, the good version, the one from the freezer list on the door, which is exactly what it's there for. Answered one urgent message, about a contract question, and otherwise stayed offline. Delegated the vendor call, which I guess counts as progress. Chloe took it. She did fine, of course. She sent me a two-line summary and said, go back to sleep. So I did. Priya left a bag of throat lozenges and ginger ale on my doorknob with a note that said, eat it before it dies. Full circle, again.
entries.highlight: Took a sick day, stayed offline, ate freezer soup, and delegated a vendor call to Chloe.

entries.title: Planning Thanksgiving
entries.body: Booked train tickets to my parents' for Thanksgiving this morning, the Wednesday 3:10 like last year, back on Saturday. $64 round trip, already in the budget sheet. Mom called this afternoon and assigned me the stuffing and a pie, same as every year. This year she said, the crust is yours, I trust you, which is the first time she's ever said that about anything in the kitchen. I almost dropped the phone. Made a grocery list for the week before so I am not scrambling: butter, flour, apples, sage, celery, onions, sourdough from the market, and, at the very top, in capital letters, nothing to forget. Dad got on the phone at the end and said he'll do the walk with me Thanksgiving morning, a full mile and a half, before the food. Two years ago, I couldn't run six minutes around his block. Now we're walking it together.
entries.highlight: Booked train tickets home for Thanksgiving, was assigned the stuffing and pie by Mom, and made a grocery list in advance.

entries.title: Low-energy Saturday
entries.body: Slept until 10 and still felt tired. I think the whole month caught up with me: the launch, the 1:1, the workshop, the building dinner, and the dark mornings. Skipped the grocery run and ordered delivery instead, which cost $18 more than the store would have, but I'm counting it as a rest expense. Did a short walk around the block in the afternoon, just to see the sky, and it helped a little. The maples are mostly bare now. I'm trying not to read this as the start of a slump, like last year. Last year one tired day turned into a tired season. This year I think it's just one tired Saturday after a very big month. There's a difference, and I know it now. Going to try going to bed earlier this week, 10pm every night, with the light lamp in the morning. And I booked two swims. I'll go.
entries.highlight: Felt tired after a big month, rested, ordered delivery, and took a short walk while planning earlier bedtimes to avoid a winter slump.

entries.title: Work-from-home Friday
entries.body: Worked from the couch with the window open, since it was a weirdly warm 63 degrees for November, and the light came across the floor all morning. Got through a full draft of the onboarding spec without meetings. I blocked the whole day and nobody fought me on it. Here's the delegating part, right after my review: I didn't write the whole thing. I wrote the structure and the problem statements from the workshop, and I left three sections blank with names on them. Chloe has the research plan, Tomas has the first week flow, and Ravi has the metrics. I felt the itch to fill them in myself, and I didn't. Took a real lunch break and walked to the bakery by the lake. Spinach and feta, the usual, and the woman said, the usual? before I even got to the counter. Ate on the bench. Then back to the couch, and at 5, I closed the laptop.
entries.highlight: Worked from home on a full draft of the onboarding spec, deliberately leaving sections for teammates, and took a real lunch break.

entries.title: Ran my first design workshop
entries.body: Led a 90-minute workshop for the onboarding redesign. It's official now, Dana confirmed the Q4 plan last week, and this was the first real step. Twenty-two people from design, engineering, product, support, and sales. I was nervous for the first ten minutes, talking a little too fast, and my hands were shaking holding the marker. Then I put up the grid of thirty-one empty state screens from February 2025, and the drop-off chart Ravi made in January, and everyone started talking at once, and then it got fun. Chloe ran the sticky note exercise, and Tomas took notes. We ended up with three clear problem statements, written on the whiteboard in big letters, that everyone agreed on. And the sales team actually showed up, all four of them, which never happens, and they had the best stories about customers getting lost. Elena took a photo of the whiteboard. I'm going to frame it, metaphorically.
entries.highlight: Led their first 90-minute design workshop for the onboarding redesign, producing three clear problem statements with broad attendance.
